ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4017.q: Actual unemployment is 8%. An estimate puts frictional unemployment at 2% and structural unemployment at 3%. Which decomposition and policy limit are consistent?
options: Natural unemployment is zero and cyclical unemployment 8 points; full employment requires everyone to have a job
Natural unemployment is 5% and cyclical unemployment 3 points; removing weak demand need not remove the remaining 5%
Natural unemployment is 8% and cyclical unemployment zero; every observed rate is the natural rate
Natural unemployment is 3% and cyclical unemployment 5 points; frictional search is excluded
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4017.$correct: Natural unemployment is 5% and cyclical unemployment 3 points; removing weak demand need not remove the remaining 5%
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4017.feedback: The natural benchmark is frictional plus structural: 2+3=5%. Actual minus natural is 8−5=3 points. Eliminating the cyclical gap does not eliminate matching or structural unemployment.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4017.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Natural unemployment is zero and cyclical unemployment 8 points; full employment requires everyone to have a job” in this natural rate of unemployment task.

ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4033.q: A recovery reduces actual unemployment among workers while job-matching institutions and skill mismatch are unchanged. An analyst says the natural rate must have fallen by the same amount. Which evidence corrects the inference?
options: Any fall in actual unemployment mechanically lowers the natural rate, regardless of institutions
The natural rate rises whenever actual unemployment falls because the two rates sum to a constant
The natural rate equals zero once a recession ends, regardless of persistent job search
The cyclical gap may shrink with an unchanged natural rate; changes in frictional/structural conditions are separate evidence
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4033.$correct: The cyclical gap may shrink with an unchanged natural rate; changes in frictional/structural conditions are separate evidence
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4033.feedback: Actual unemployment reflects both the natural benchmark and cyclical conditions. Recovery can reduce the latter without changing the former.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4033.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Any fall in actual unemployment mechanically lowers the natural rate, regardless of institutions” in this natural rate of unemployment task.

ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4034.q: A reform improves matching for 120 job seekers but rapid technology change creates new skill mismatches. What can be inferred about the natural rate before their magnitudes are known?
options: Only actual unemployment can change; the natural benchmark is fixed by definition
The natural rate must rise because structural changes always dominate frictional changes
Better matching lowers its frictional component while mismatch raises its structural component; net change is uncertain
Both changes lower the natural rate because all technology improves job matching
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4034.$correct: Better matching lowers its frictional component while mismatch raises its structural component; net change is uncertain
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4034.feedback: The natural rate is not immutable. It combines frictional and structural components, and opposing component changes require magnitudes to sign their sum.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4034.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Only actual unemployment can change; the natural benchmark is fixed by definition” in this natural rate of unemployment task.

ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4035.q: Actual unemployment is 4% and the estimated natural rate is 5% in a labor market. Expected inflation has not yet adapted. Which interpretation and longer-run caution follow?
options: Unemployment must become zero as expectations adjust because the gap is negative
A temporary negative cyclical gap is possible; it does not establish a permanently lower natural rate
The data are impossible because actual unemployment can never fall below its natural rate
The natural rate must immediately become 4% because it is defined as actual unemployment
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4035.$correct: A temporary negative cyclical gap is possible; it does not establish a permanently lower natural rate
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4035.feedback: Actual unemployment can temporarily be below the natural benchmark during strong demand. Expectations and wages can adjust; without changed labor-market structure, that does not prove a lower natural rate.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4035.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Unemployment must become zero as expectations adjust because the gap is negative” in this natural rate of unemployment task.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9130.q: In the labor market, retraining reduces structural unemployment while a recession increases cyclical unemployment. The measured rate is unchanged. Which inference is valid?
options: The natural rate is unchanged because every structural change must appear in the measured rate
The natural rate rises because a recession changes only structural unemployment
Retraining had no effect because actual unemployment did not fall
The natural rate can fall even with unchanged actual unemployment because the cyclical gap increased
ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9130.$correct: The natural rate can fall even with unchanged actual unemployment because the cyclical gap increased
ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9130.feedback: Actual unemployment can be unchanged when a lower structural/natural component is offset by a larger cyclical gap. An unchanged total does not prove unchanged components.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9130.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The natural rate is unchanged because every structural change must appear in the measured rate” in this natural rate of unemployment task.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9131.q: Actual unemployment falls from 8% to 5%. During the same period retraining lowers structural unemployment from 3% to 2%, while frictional unemployment stays 2%. Which decomposition avoids crediting the whole decline to demand recovery?
options: Natural: 5%→5%; cyclical: 3%→0%; demand recovery explains the entire decline.
Natural: 3%→2%; cyclical: 5%→3%; frictional unemployment belongs in the cyclical component.
Natural: 5%→4%; cyclical: 3%→1%; reform and demand recovery both contribute.
Natural: 5%→2%; cyclical: 3%→3%; structural reform explains the entire decline.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9131.$correct: Natural: 5%→4%; cyclical: 3%→1%; reform and demand recovery both contribute.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9131.feedback: Before: natural 2+3=5 and cyclical 8−5=3. After: natural 2+2=4 and cyclical 5−4=1. One point comes from the natural-rate change and two from the cyclical decline.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9131.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Natural unemployment falls 3%→1%; all remaining joblessness is frictional” in this natural rate of unemployment task.

PM2B4-NRU-EB-001.q: Demand returns to normal and actual unemployment equals the estimated natural rate. A proposal calls for more demand stimulus to eliminate the remaining frictional and structural unemployment. Which limitation matters?
options: Further demand directly supplies missing skills; the natural rate falls with every spending increase.
Equality with natural unemployment means nobody is searching; all remaining unemployment is a data error.
Further demand removes frictional search by definition; inflation remains fixed after expectations adjust.
Further demand cannot reliably remove matching and skill frictions; it may instead raise inflation pressure.
PM2B4-NRU-EB-001.$correct: Further demand cannot reliably remove matching and skill frictions; it may instead raise inflation pressure.
PM2B4-NRU-EB-001.feedback: At the natural rate the cyclical gap has closed, but job search and skill mismatches remain. Sustained demand stimulus does not by itself repair those real labor-market mechanisms and can generate inflationary pressure.
PM2B4-NRU-EB-001.commonError: Incorrect inference: Further demand directly supplies missing skills; the natural rate falls with every spending increase.

PM2B4-NRU-EB-002.q: A reform improves matching for 170 job seekers but rapid technology change creates new skill mismatches. What can be inferred about the natural rate before their magnitudes are known?
options: Only actual unemployment can change; the natural benchmark is fixed by definition
The natural rate must rise because structural changes always dominate frictional changes
Better matching lowers its frictional component while mismatch raises its structural component; net change is uncertain
Both changes lower the natural rate because all technology improves job matching
PM2B4-NRU-EB-002.$correct: Better matching lowers its frictional component while mismatch raises its structural component; net change is uncertain
PM2B4-NRU-EB-002.feedback: The natural rate is not immutable. It combines frictional and structural components, and opposing component changes require magnitudes to sign their sum.
PM2B4-NRU-EB-002.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Only actual unemployment can change; the natural benchmark is fixed by definition” in this natural rate of unemployment task.

PM2B4-NRU-EB-003.q: Actual unemployment remains 4% while new evidence lowers the estimated natural rate from 5% to 4%. Holding other influences fixed, what changes in the diagnosis of demand pressure?
options: The natural rate stays 5%; observations of actual unemployment cannot inform its estimation.
The negative unemployment gap closes; the earlier excess-demand diagnosis is no longer implied.
The negative unemployment gap doubles; a lower natural rate intensifies the measured demand boom.
The actual rate rises to 5%; revising an estimate changes the count of unemployed people.
PM2B4-NRU-EB-003.$correct: The negative unemployment gap closes; the earlier excess-demand diagnosis is no longer implied.
PM2B4-NRU-EB-003.feedback: The gap is actual minus natural: initially 4−5=−1 point, then 4−4=0. Revised evidence about the natural benchmark changes the demand-pressure interpretation without changing measured actual unemployment.
PM2B4-NRU-EB-003.commonError: Incorrect inference: The negative unemployment gap doubles; a lower natural rate intensifies the measured demand boom.

PM2B4-NRU-LB-001.q: Retraining lowers structural unemployment, but actual unemployment stays unchanged during a slump. Frictional unemployment is unchanged. What follows for the cyclical unemployment gap?
options: It widens by the natural-rate decline; unchanged actual unemployment conceals offsetting changes.
It narrows by the natural-rate decline; retraining directly removes the demand shortfall.
It stays unchanged; actual unemployment fixes every component separately.
It disappears; lower structural unemployment establishes full recovery despite unchanged actual unemployment.
PM2B4-NRU-LB-001.$correct: It widens by the natural-rate decline; unchanged actual unemployment conceals offsetting changes.
PM2B4-NRU-LB-001.feedback: Natural unemployment falls when structural unemployment falls and frictional unemployment is fixed. Actual minus natural therefore rises by the same amount if actual unemployment is unchanged.
PM2B4-NRU-LB-001.commonError: Incorrect inference: It narrows by the natural-rate decline; retraining directly removes the demand shortfall.

PM2B4-NRU-MB-004.q: An economy has frictional unemployment 2%, structural 3% and actual 6%. If a demand recovery removes the cyclical component without changing matching or skills, which rate remains and why?
options: 5%; frictional and structural remain after the cyclical point disappears.
0%; removing cyclical unemployment also removes frictional and structural components.
3%; frictional unemployment disappears with the cyclical component during recovery.
6%; changes in demand leave all three unemployment components unchanged.
PM2B4-NRU-MB-004.$correct: 5%; frictional and structural remain after the cyclical point disappears.
PM2B4-NRU-MB-004.feedback: Natural unemployment=2+3=5; the initial cyclical component is 6−5=1. Recovery alone does not remove search and structural mismatch.
PM2B4-NRU-MB-004.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “0%; eliminating cyclical unemployment eliminates every component” in this natural rate of unemployment task.

PM2B4-NRU-MB-005.q: Actual unemployment and the estimated natural rate both fall after demand recovery and a matching reform. What information separates the two contributions?
options: The final actual rate alone; it identifies both reform and demand contributions.
The inflation rate alone; it directly measures each unemployment component.
The initial labor force alone; unchanged population fixes both contributions.
Changes in the natural rate and in actual minus natural unemployment.
PM2B4-NRU-MB-005.$correct: Changes in the natural rate and in actual minus natural unemployment.
PM2B4-NRU-MB-005.feedback: The natural-rate change captures changed frictional/structural conditions. The change in actual unemployment minus the natural rate captures the cyclical component. Both are needed when reform and recovery occur together.
PM2B4-NRU-MB-005.commonError: Incorrect inference: The final actual rate alone; it identifies both reform and demand contributions.

PM2B4-NRU-MB-006.q: A reform improves matching for 220 job seekers but rapid technology change creates new skill mismatches. What can be inferred about the natural rate before their magnitudes are known?
options: Only actual unemployment can change; the natural benchmark is fixed by definition
The natural rate must rise because structural changes always dominate frictional changes
Better matching lowers its frictional component while mismatch raises its structural component; net change is uncertain
Both changes lower the natural rate because all technology improves job matching
PM2B4-NRU-MB-006.$correct: Better matching lowers its frictional component while mismatch raises its structural component; net change is uncertain
PM2B4-NRU-MB-006.feedback: The natural rate is not immutable. It combines frictional and structural components, and opposing component changes require magnitudes to sign their sum.
PM2B4-NRU-MB-006.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Only actual unemployment can change; the natural benchmark is fixed by definition” in this natural rate of unemployment task.

ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4014.q: A binding wage floor raises pay for retained workers in a competitive labor market, but firms offer fewer jobs and more people seek work at the higher wage. Which evaluation addresses both margins?
options: Retained wages rise, jobs become scarcer; total earnings depend on quantities.
Retained wages rise, jobs become scarcer; total earnings rise by the wage percentage.
Retained wages rise, jobs become scarcer; total earnings fall by the employment percentage.
Retained wages rise, jobs expand; the higher wage signals a demand increase.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4014.$correct: Retained wages rise, jobs become scarcer; total earnings depend on quantities.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4014.feedback: A binding floor changes the wage paid and the quantity employed along demand. Winners among retained workers do not establish an aggregate earnings gain; employment quantities matter.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4014.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “All workers necessarily gain equal income because the legal wage is higher” in this labor market institutions task.

ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4021.q: A firm voluntarily pays above the market wage to reduce turnover and improve effort among workers. Which comparison distinguishes an efficiency wage from a union-negotiated wage without denying either employment tradeoff?
options: Firm incentives drive efficiency wages; bargaining drives union wages; only unions can exceed clearing.
Bargaining drives efficiency wages; firm incentives drive union wages; either can exceed clearing.
Firm incentives drive efficiency wages; bargaining drives union wages; either can exceed clearing.
Legal wage floors drive both wage types; neither depends on productivity or bargaining.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4021.$correct: Firm incentives drive efficiency wages; bargaining drives union wages; either can exceed clearing.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4021.feedback: Efficiency wages arise from employer incentives such as effort and turnover; union wages arise from bargaining. They differ in mechanism even if both can leave job seekers unmatched at the wage.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4021.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The wage is a government price ceiling; it increases labor demand by legal requirement” in this labor market institutions task.

ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4022.q: A benefit reform gives 120 unemployed workers more time to search for good matches. Search duration rises, while later job retention also improves. Which policy assessment recognizes the tradeoff?
options: Longer search raises frictional costs; better retention adds nothing; welfare necessarily falls.
Longer search raises frictional costs; better retention adds benefits; welfare needs both.
Better retention adds benefits; longer search adds no cost; welfare necessarily rises.
Longer search is cyclical; better retention is structural; frictional costs remain unchanged.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4022.$correct: Longer search raises frictional costs; better retention adds benefits; welfare needs both.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4022.feedback: Search incentives and match quality can move in opposite evaluative directions. A longer spell need not mean the eventual match is worse; welfare assessment needs both costs and benefits.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4022.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both observations imply cyclical unemployment rose because matching institutions affect only demand” in this labor market institutions task.

ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4024.q: Job-search assistance speeds matching for 130 applicants, while reduced search pressure permits others to wait longer for suitable offers. Which unemployment prediction requires more evidence?
options: Whether either channel concerns frictional unemployment; all search is structural by definition
Whether faster matching reduces a spell, because matching can affect only wages
Whether weaker search pressure raises the natural rate permanently regardless of matching gains
The net frictional-unemployment change, because faster matching and longer chosen searches oppose
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4024.$correct: The net frictional-unemployment change, because faster matching and longer chosen searches oppose
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4024.feedback: Faster matching shortens spells; waiting longer can lengthen them. Both involve the search component, so relative magnitudes are needed for the net rate.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4024.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Whether either channel concerns frictional unemployment; all search is structural by definition” in this labor market institutions task.

ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4025.q: Above-market wages improve effort among 140 retained employees. A proposal predicts that productivity gains must exactly offset reduced hiring. Which missing comparison is essential?
options: Whether the statutory unemployment denominator should exclude workers receiving higher wages
Whether every firm uses identical technology, which alone guarantees an exact offset
The size of the productivity/turnover benefit relative to the higher labor cost and hiring response
Whether retained employees are classified as unemployed when the wage is above equilibrium
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4025.$correct: The size of the productivity/turnover benefit relative to the higher labor cost and hiring response
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4025.feedback: The efficiency mechanism can benefit the employer, but it does not algebraically guarantee a particular employment or cost offset. Relative magnitudes determine the net result.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4025.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Whether the statutory unemployment denominator should exclude workers receiving higher wages” in this labor market institutions task.

ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4026.q: At a binding wage floor, 120 workers seek jobs and firms hire 90. A productivity gain raises hiring to 110 with the wage and labor supply unchanged. Which claim about the labor surplus is correct?
options: Surplus falls from 30 to zero; increased demand fully removes the wage-floor constraint.
Surplus falls from 30 to 10; twenty additional jobs leave ten unfilled requests.
Surplus rises from 10 to 30; productivity gains displace twenty previously employed workers.
Surplus stays at 30; the unchanged wage fixes the number of available jobs.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4026.$correct: Surplus falls from 30 to 10; twenty additional jobs leave ten unfilled requests.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4026.feedback: Surplus initially 120−90=30, later 120−110=10. The fixed wage does not prevent labor demand changing; the remaining positive surplus still matters.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4026.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “It disappears because any increase in hiring eliminates a binding wage floor” in this labor market institutions task.

ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4027.q: A nonunion firm pays above the clearing wage to reduce quits. Turnover falls but hiring also falls. Which evaluation separates the intended mechanism from the employment tradeoff?
options: Retention benefits can coexist with fewer jobs; above-clearing efficiency pay can ration employment.
Lower turnover proves employment increased; retention and hiring measure the same margin.
Fewer jobs prove the wage was union-imposed; a firm cannot choose efficiency pay.
Lower turnover eliminates rationing; an efficiency wage necessarily clears the labor market.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4027.$correct: Retention benefits can coexist with fewer jobs; above-clearing efficiency pay can ration employment.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4027.feedback: An efficiency wage is chosen for productivity or retention incentives. Those benefits do not establish that all willing workers obtain jobs at the higher wage; lower hiring is a separate margin in the policy evaluation.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4027.commonError: Incorrect inference: Lower turnover proves employment increased; retention and hiring measure the same margin.

ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4028.q: A benefit reform gives 170 unemployed workers more time to search for good matches. Search duration rises, while later job retention also improves. Which policy assessment recognizes the tradeoff?
options: Longer search raises frictional costs; better retention adds nothing; welfare necessarily falls.
Better retention adds benefits; longer search adds no cost; welfare necessarily rises.
Longer search is cyclical; better retention is structural; frictional costs remain unchanged.
Longer search raises frictional costs; better retention adds benefits; welfare needs both.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4028.$correct: Longer search raises frictional costs; better retention adds benefits; welfare needs both.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4028.feedback: Search incentives and match quality can move in opposite evaluative directions. A longer spell need not mean the eventual match is worse; welfare assessment needs both costs and benefits.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4028.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Longer search proves the reform reduced job-match quality despite better observed retention” in this labor market institutions task.

ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4029.q: Job-search assistance speeds matching for 180 applicants, while reduced search pressure permits others to wait longer for suitable offers. Which unemployment prediction requires more evidence?
options: Whether faster matching reduces a spell, because matching can affect only wages
Whether weaker search pressure raises the natural rate permanently regardless of matching gains
The net frictional-unemployment change, because faster matching and longer chosen searches oppose
Whether either channel concerns frictional unemployment; all search is structural by definition
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4029.$correct: The net frictional-unemployment change, because faster matching and longer chosen searches oppose
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4029.feedback: Faster matching shortens spells; waiting longer can lengthen them. Both involve the search component, so relative magnitudes are needed for the net rate.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4029.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Whether faster matching reduces a spell, because matching can affect only wages” in this labor market institutions task.

ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4030.q: Above-market wages improve effort among 190 retained employees. A proposal predicts that productivity gains must exactly offset reduced hiring. Which missing comparison is essential?
options: Whether the statutory unemployment denominator should exclude workers receiving higher wages
Whether every firm uses identical technology, which alone guarantees an exact offset
The size of the productivity/turnover benefit relative to the higher labor cost and hiring response
Whether retained employees are classified as unemployed when the wage is above equilibrium
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4030.$correct: The size of the productivity/turnover benefit relative to the higher labor cost and hiring response

ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4031.q: A firm voluntarily raises wages above market rates. Its wage bill rises $12,000, turnover costs fall $8,000 and improved effort adds $7,000 to revenue. Which evaluation goes beyond looking only at wages?
options: Profit falls $3,000 because cost savings reduce revenue
Profit rises $3,000 under these estimates; the efficiency gains exceed the wage cost
Profit falls $12,000 because only payroll affects profitability
Profit rises $15,000 because higher payroll is not a cost
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4031.$correct: Profit rises $3,000 under these estimates; the efficiency gains exceed the wage cost
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4031.feedback: Net profit change=−12000+8000+7000=3000. The stated efficiency-wage channels can justify higher pay; that is conditional on the estimates.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4031.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Profit falls $3,000 because cost savings reduce revenue” in this labor market institutions task.

ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4032.q: Better monitoring lets a firm obtain the same effort at a lower wage. A proposal instead keeps its old above-market wage solely to deter shirking. Which inference follows from the changed constraint?
options: The efficiency-wage premium may become less valuable; monitoring substitutes for part of its incentive role.
The efficiency-wage premium must rise; monitoring raises the minimum wage set by law.
The union wage must rise; monitoring automatically creates collective bargaining coverage.
The market-clearing wage becomes irrelevant; a lower effort cost fixes employment mechanically.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4032.$correct: The efficiency-wage premium may become less valuable; monitoring substitutes for part of its incentive role.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4032.feedback: If monitoring delivers the same effort at lower pay, part of the original anti-shirking reason for a wage premium weakens. The observation does not establish a legal or union wage requirement or a mechanical employment change.
ECON-NL-FINALBOSS-4032.commonError: Incorrect inference: The efficiency-wage premium must rise; monitoring raises the minimum wage set by law.

PM2B4-LMI-EB-001.q: A union agreement raises members’ wages while firms reduce hiring. A report measures only the wage gain of those still employed. Which additional evidence is needed to evaluate the employment tradeoff?
options: Only the union’s name, because unemployment is unrelated to the contract
Whether the wage is nominal, because real wages cannot affect labor demand
How many workers lose or cannot obtain jobs under the higher wage
Only the price level, because hiring cannot change at an agreed wage
PM2B4-LMI-EB-001.$correct: How many workers lose or cannot obtain jobs under the higher wage
PM2B4-LMI-EB-001.feedback: The report conditions on remaining employed and omits workers excluded from jobs. Assessing the tradeoff requires both wage gains and the employment margin.
PM2B4-LMI-EB-001.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Only the union’s name, because unemployment is unrelated to the contract” in this labor market institutions task.

PM2B4-LMI-EB-002.q: A union negotiates an above-market wage, while a nonunion firm voluntarily offers the same premium to reduce turnover. Does equal observed pay establish the same wage-setting mechanism?
options: No; the union wage is a price ceiling while voluntary pay is a price floor.
No; collective bargaining and employer retention incentives can produce the same observed wage.
Yes; any above-market wage establishes collective bargaining in both workplaces.
Yes; equal wages establish identical productivity and turnover effects in both workplaces.
PM2B4-LMI-EB-002.$correct: No; collective bargaining and employer retention incentives can produce the same observed wage.
PM2B4-LMI-EB-002.feedback: The same wage can arise through different mechanisms. A union bargains on behalf of members; an employer may independently choose efficiency pay to improve retention. The wage level alone does not identify the mechanism or all outcomes.
PM2B4-LMI-EB-002.commonError: Incorrect inference: Yes; any above-market wage establishes collective bargaining in both workplaces.

Better retention adds benefits; longer search adds no cost; welfare necessarily rises.

options: Whether retained employees are classified as unemployed when the wage is above equilibrium

Whether every firm uses identical technology, which alone guarantees an exact offset

PM2B4-LMI-MB-005.q: A minimum wage of $12 is proposed where the competitive equilibrium wage is $15. A forecast predicts a labor surplus solely because a legal minimum exists. Which condition is missing?
options: The floor must be below equilibrium to create excess labor supply
A wage floor creates excess labor demand even when it does not bind
The floor must bind; a $12 minimum does not constrain the stated $15 equilibrium
Any wage floor binds because it is set by law
PM2B4-LMI-MB-005.$correct: The floor must bind; a $12 minimum does not constrain the stated $15 equilibrium
PM2B4-LMI-MB-005.feedback: The usual surplus prediction requires a wage above equilibrium. This floor does not prevent the competitive equilibrium, so the claimed effect does not follow.
PM2B4-LMI-MB-005.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The floor must be below equilibrium to create excess labor supply” in this labor market institutions task.

PM2B4-LMI-MB-006.q: A firm claims higher pay is profitable because it cuts turnover costs. What comparison tests that claim rather than assuming any wage premium pays for itself?
options: Compare posted wages across firms alone; a higher wage establishes higher profit.
Compare added wage expense with reduced turnover costs and any productivity gain.
Compare the wage with the legal minimum alone; retention costs cannot affect profit.
Compare headcounts alone; wage expense and worker productivity do not affect profit.
PM2B4-LMI-MB-006.$correct: Compare added wage expense with reduced turnover costs and any productivity gain.
PM2B4-LMI-MB-006.feedback: The efficiency-wage claim is behavioral, not an accounting identity. The firm must weigh the extra wage bill against lower hiring/training costs from quits and any productivity benefit; a premium alone does not prove profitability.
PM2B4-LMI-MB-006.commonError: Incorrect inference: Compare the wage with the legal minimum alone; retention costs cannot affect profit.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9118.q: A plant initially produces 1000 units in 100 labor hours. Output later rises 20% while hours rise 25%. Which finding corrects the manager's claim that output growth proves higher labor productivity?
options: Output per hour falls 25% because the output increase is irrelevant
Total output rises, but output per hour falls 4%
Both total output and output per hour rise 20%
Output per hour rises 5% because hours grow faster than output
ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9118.$correct: Total output rises, but output per hour falls 4%
ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9118.feedback: Productivity is output/hours. Its change factor is 1.20/1.25 = 0.96, a 4% decline despite more output.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9118.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Output per hour falls 25% because the output increase is irrelevant” in this productivity measurement task.

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3006.q: A firm produces 1100 units at 10 units per labor hour. After training, productivity is 12 units per hour and required output rises to 1320. Which conclusion follows about labor hours and its limit?
options: Hours are zero; higher productivity replaces all labor
Hours remain 110; higher output exactly matches the proportional productivity gain
Hours rise to 132; output growth alone sets required hours
Hours fall to 91.7; apply the productivity gain but ignore higher required output
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3006.$correct: Hours remain 110; higher output exactly matches the proportional productivity gain
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3006.feedback: Initial hours = 1100/10 = 110; new hours = 1320/12 = 110. Productivity gains do not necessarily reduce total hours when output demand changes too.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3006.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Hours are zero; higher productivity replaces all labor” in this productivity measurement task.

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3007.q: Two plants produce the same 1200 units. Plant A uses 120 hours and B uses 240 hours. B then cuts hours by 40% without changing output. Which comparison is correct?
options: B's productivity rises 66.7% and remains below A's.
B's productivity rises 40% and reaches A's level.
B's productivity falls 40% and remains below A's.
B's productivity rises 100% and exceeds A's level.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3007.$correct: B's productivity rises 66.7% and remains below A's.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3007.feedback: B initially produces 5 units/hour; after hours fall to 60%, productivity is 5/0.6≈8.33, a 66.7% gain but still below A's 10.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3007.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “B's productivity rises 40% and equals A's productivity” in this productivity measurement task.

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3008.q: In an economy, Output per hour rises 5%, average hours per worker falls 5%, and employment is unchanged. Which distinction matters for total output?
options: Hourly productivity rises 5%; total output rises 5%.
Hourly productivity rises 5%; total output is unchanged.
Hourly productivity falls 5%; total output falls 5%.
Hourly productivity rises 5%; total output falls 0.25%.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3008.$correct: Hourly productivity rises 5%; total output falls 0.25%.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3008.feedback: Total output is output/hour × hours/worker × workers. The change factor is 1.05×0.95 = 0.9975, a 0.25% decline. Equal opposite percentages do not cancel multiplicatively.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3008.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Output rises exactly 5% because productivity alone determines total output” in this productivity measurement task.

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3009.q: Output per worker rises in a firm with 140 employees, but average hours per worker also rises. Which additional evidence is needed to infer output-per-hour growth?
options: Observe that nominal wages rose; that establishes output per hour rose
Observe that total output rose; that establishes output per hour rose
Compare the percentage output-per-worker change with the percentage hours-per-worker change
Compare only employee head count; longer hours never affect hourly productivity

PM2B3-PROD-EB-001.q: Two plants produce the same 1700 units. Plant A uses 170 hours and B uses 340 hours. B then cuts hours by 40% without changing output. Which comparison is correct?

PM2B3-PROD-EB-003.q: Output per hour rises 5% and average hours per worker falls 5%. What employment change would keep total output exactly unchanged, rather than merely approximately unchanged?

PM2B3-PROD-EB-003.commonError: Incorrect inference: Employment is unchanged; equal opposite percentage changes cancel exactly.

ECON-EC-LEGENDARYBOSS-20018.q: Country A begins at $40110 real GDP per person and grows 2% annually; B begins at half that level and grows 7%. Using the Rule of 70, which warning corrects the claim that B catches A in ten years?
options: B doubles in ten years; A's starting level establishes catch-up then.
A doubles in ten years; B doubles in thirty-five, preventing catch-up.
B doubles in five years; doubling its growth rate halves catch-up time.
B doubles in ten years; A also grows, delaying catch-up.
ECON-EC-LEGENDARYBOSS-20018.$correct: B doubles in ten years; A also grows, delaying catch-up.
ECON-EC-LEGENDARYBOSS-20018.feedback: 70/7≈10 years doubles B's starting level; 70/2≈35 years doubles A's. A is a moving target, so B reaching A's initial level is not the same as reaching A's contemporaneous level.
ECON-EC-LEGENDARYBOSS-20018.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “B doubles in about thirty-five years, while A doubles in ten, so catch-up is immediate” in this living standards and growth task.

ECON-EC-MEDIUMBOSS-18006.q: Two countries each report $120 billion GDP. One has twice the population and a 20% higher price level. The GDP figures are nominal. Which comparison is justified before a living-standard ranking?
options: Use equal nominal totals to infer equal real output per person.
Adjust for prices and population before comparing real output per person.
Adjust for population alone; nominal price differences do not affect the comparison.
Adjust for prices alone; population differences do not affect per-person output.

ECON-EC-MEDIUMBOSS-18006.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Use equal totals as proof of equal average living standards” in this living standards and growth task.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9116.q: Real GDP per person rises from $130 to $143, but gains accrue mainly to a small group. Which inference distinguishes an average from individual outcomes?

No real output grew because not everyone gained equally
Average real output falls if the largest gains go to high-income people
Average real output rises 10%; the typical person's gain requires distributional evidence

ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9116.feedback: The aggregate per-capita ratio rises 10%, but that does not identify every person's income or the median. Distribution is additional evidence, not part of the arithmetic average.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9116.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Every person's real income rises 10% because the average rises 10%” in this living standards and growth task.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9117.q: A country with initial real GDP per person $140 sustains 4% growth instead of 2%. Another policy raises the level once by 4% but leaves later growth at 2%. Which comparison recognizes the long-run distinction?
options: Sustained growth changes only the level; the level increase shortens subsequent doubling time.
Both shorten subsequent doubling time equally; each policy specifies the same 4% figure.
Sustained growth compounds faster; the level increase leaves subsequent doubling time unchanged.
Neither changes the future path; percentage changes affect nominal measures rather than output.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9117.$correct: Sustained growth compounds faster; the level increase leaves subsequent doubling time unchanged.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9117.feedback: A growth-rate change repeatedly changes the path, whereas a one-time level gain shifts the starting point. Under Rule of 70, sustained 4% growth implies roughly 17.5-year doubling versus 35 at 2%.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9117.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The one-time gain permanently doubles the growth rate by arithmetic identity” in this living standards and growth task.

ECON-EC-FINALBOSS-19010.q: A factory buys more machines, while another trains workers to maintain its existing machines. Which distinction and implication are sound?
options: Machines add physical capital; training adds human capital; either can raise productivity.
Both add physical capital; improved maintenance counts as additional machine stock.
Machines add human capital; training adds physical capital; either can raise productivity.
Machines add physical capital; training adds labor quantity; only machines affect productivity.
ECON-EC-FINALBOSS-19010.$correct: Machines add physical capital; training adds human capital; either can raise productivity.
ECON-EC-FINALBOSS-19010.feedback: Equipment is physical capital; skills are human capital. Both can raise productive ability per worker, though their returns and implementation differ.
ECON-EC-FINALBOSS-19010.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both add physical capital because all productivity improvements are machines” in this sources of productivity task.

ECON-EC-FINALBOSS-19011.q: A fixed technology gives an extra 110 units of output from the first additional machine and only 55 from the second. A proposal assumes each later machine adds the first machine's amount. What is the flaw?
options: It ignores declining total output; the second machine reduces production.
It ignores labor displacement; the second machine must halve employment.
It ignores technical progress; each machine raises future marginal gains.
It ignores diminishing marginal gains; total output can still rise.
ECON-EC-FINALBOSS-19011.$correct: It ignores diminishing marginal gains; total output can still rise.
ECON-EC-FINALBOSS-19011.feedback: With other inputs and technology fixed, added capital can increase total output at a decreasing rate. A smaller positive increment is not a fall in total output.
ECON-EC-FINALBOSS-19011.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “It confuses diminishing returns with falling total output; the second machine necessarily destroys output” in this sources of productivity task.

ECON-EC-LEGENDARYBOSS-20020.q: Two economies each employ 120 workers. One has little capital per worker and the other much more, with similar technology and institutions. Which qualification should accompany a catch-up prediction?
options: The capital-rich economy must have higher percentage growth because its output level is higher
Equal worker counts require equal output per worker regardless of capital
The capital-poor economy may earn higher marginal returns, but investment and effective use of capital are still required
The capital-poor economy must grow faster regardless of investment, institutions or technology access
ECON-EC-LEGENDARYBOSS-20020.$correct: The capital-poor economy may earn higher marginal returns, but investment and effective use of capital are still required
ECON-EC-LEGENDARYBOSS-20020.feedback: Diminishing returns can create catch-up potential when conditions are comparable. Potential is not an automatic growth guarantee without investment and productive use.
ECON-EC-LEGENDARYBOSS-20020.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The capital-rich economy must have higher percentage growth because its output level is higher” in this sources of productivity task.

ECON-EC-MEDIUMBOSS-18007.q: A discovery increases available mineral resources for 130 workers, but extraction technology and transport remain inadequate. Which policy diagnosis best connects resources to productivity?
options: The resource expands potential opportunities, but complementary technology/infrastructure can be the binding constraint
The resource alone guarantees an immediate proportional increase in output per worker
Transport affects consumption only and cannot limit production from resources
Resource abundance makes worker skills and institutions irrelevant to long-run output
ECON-EC-MEDIUMBOSS-18007.$correct: The resource expands potential opportunities, but complementary technology/infrastructure can be the binding constraint
ECON-EC-MEDIUMBOSS-18007.feedback: Natural resources can support production, but usable technology, skills and infrastructure determine whether they can be exploited productively. More resources alone need not raise current output.
ECON-EC-MEDIUMBOSS-18007.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The resource alone guarantees an immediate proportional increase in output per worker” in this sources of productivity task.

ECON-EC-MEDIUMBOSS-18022.feedback: Better methods change what existing inputs can produce. Physical-capital accumulation and technological knowledge are distinct channels, and either can affect productivity.
ECON-EC-MEDIUMBOSS-18022.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The gain must be more labor because technology is not an input to productive capacity” in this sources of productivity task.

options: The resource alone guarantees an immediate proportional increase in output per worker
Transport affects consumption only and cannot limit production from resources
Resource abundance makes worker skills and institutions irrelevant to long-run output
The resource expands potential opportunities, but complementary technology/infrastructure can be the binding constraint
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3013.$correct: The resource expands potential opportunities, but complementary technology/infrastructure can be the binding constraint

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3013.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The resource alone guarantees an immediate proportional increase in output per worker” in this sources of productivity task.

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3014.q: A new production method lets the same 190 workers and machines produce more output. A capital-only explanation predicts no gain because the machine stock did not rise. Which correction is right?
options: The machine stock must have risen by the same percentage as output by accounting identity
The gain can only be higher prices because unchanged machines imply unchanged real output
Technological knowledge raises productivity with existing inputs; it differs from simply accumulating more machines
The gain must be more labor because technology is not an input to productive capacity
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3014.$correct: Technological knowledge raises productivity with existing inputs; it differs from simply accumulating more machines
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3014.feedback: Better methods change what existing inputs can produce. Physical-capital accumulation and technological knowledge are distinct channels, and either can affect productivity.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3014.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The machine stock must have risen by the same percentage as output by accounting identity” in this sources of productivity task.

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3015.q: A firm licenses a better production method and separately trains staff to use it. An analyst calls both investments an increase in worker headcount. Which correction separates the two productivity channels?
options: Both add labor quantity; output per worker is unchanged by either investment.
The method improves technology; training improves human capital; neither requires more workers.
The method improves human capital; training adds physical machines; both require more workers.
Both add physical capital; worker knowledge matters only through a larger headcount.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3015.$correct: The method improves technology; training improves human capital; neither requires more workers.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3015.feedback: A usable production method changes how inputs are combined, while training changes workers' productive skills. Both can raise output per worker without increasing the number employed.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3015.commonError: Incorrect inference: The method improves human capital; training adds physical machines; both require more workers.

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3016.q: A fixed technology gives an extra 210 units of output from the first additional machine and only 105 from the second. A proposal assumes each later machine adds the first machine's amount. What is the flaw?
options: It ignores diminishing marginal gains; total output can still rise.
It ignores declining total output; the second machine reduces production.
It ignores labor displacement; the second machine must halve employment.
It ignores technical progress; each machine raises future marginal gains.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3016.$correct: It ignores diminishing marginal gains; total output can still rise.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3016.feedback: With other inputs and technology fixed, added capital can increase total output at a decreasing rate. A smaller positive increment is not a fall in total output.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3016.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “It confuses diminishing returns with falling total output; the second machine necessarily destroys output” in this sources of productivity task.

options: The capital-poor economy must grow faster regardless of investment, institutions or technology access
The capital-rich economy must have higher percentage growth because its output level is higher
Equal worker counts require equal output per worker regardless of capital

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3019.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The gain can only be higher prices because unchanged machines imply unchanged real output” in this sources of productivity task.

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3020.q: A country imports identical machines while its most skilled operators emigrate. Output per remaining worker fails to rise. Which diagnosis challenges the claim that more equipment guarantees higher productivity?
options: Technology necessarily deteriorated, since capital and skills cannot affect output per worker.
Physical capital increased, but lost human capital can offset its productivity contribution.
Physical capital decreased, since imported equipment is excluded from productive capital.
Human capital increased, since a smaller workforce automatically has more skill per worker.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3020.$correct: Physical capital increased, but lost human capital can offset its productivity contribution.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3020.feedback: Imported machines are productive physical capital even though their purchase is offset in expenditure-account GDP. Losing skilled operators can reduce effective human capital and offset the machinery's contribution; the net outcome needs both channels.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3020.commonError: Incorrect inference: Physical capital decreased, since imported equipment is excluded from productive capital.

options: It ignores diminishing marginal gains; total output can still rise.

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3025.q: Two plants use identical equipment and workforce sizes. One adopts a more effective workflow; its output per worker rises. Which inference is supported, and which remains unproved?
options: Organization can improve productivity; the observation does not establish additional physical capital.
Physical capital must have risen; organization cannot change output with fixed equipment.
Labor quantity must have risen; output per worker measures only employment changes.
Human capital must have fallen; higher output at fixed inputs implies less worker skill.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3025.$correct: Organization can improve productivity; the observation does not establish additional physical capital.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3025.feedback: Using the same equipment and workers more effectively can raise output per worker. The comparison rules out an increase in the stated machine stock and headcount; it does not require either to have grown.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3025.commonError: Incorrect inference: Physical capital must have risen; organization cannot change output with fixed equipment.

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3026.q: A fixed technology gives an extra 310 units of output from the first additional machine and only 155 from the second. A proposal assumes each later machine adds the first machine's amount. What is the flaw?
options: It ignores declining total output; the second machine reduces production.

It ignores diminishing marginal gains; total output can still rise.

PM2B3-SRC-FB-006.q: Training raises output per hour at a factory, but a reduction in operating hours leaves total output unchanged. A report says the training had no productivity benefit. Which correction follows?
options: Hourly productivity was unchanged; total output alone measures output per hour.
Hourly productivity fell; a reduction in hours directly lowers output per hour.
Physical capital must have increased; training cannot change productivity with fixed output.
Hourly productivity improved; fewer hours offset the gain in total output.
PM2B3-SRC-FB-006.$correct: Hourly productivity improved; fewer hours offset the gain in total output.
PM2B3-SRC-FB-006.feedback: Productivity and output are different measures. When output is unchanged and hours fall, output per hour rises. Lower hours can offset the total-output effect of improved skills.
PM2B3-SRC-FB-006.commonError: Incorrect inference: Hourly productivity was unchanged; total output alone measures output per hour.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9122.q: A country has idle capacity after a recession and weak long-run research incentives. Which policy pairing addresses the two different problems?
options: Research incentives instantly eliminate every current demand shortfall without a timing lag
Both problems require only more nominal money because all real output is money-determined
Demand stabilization can use idle capacity; stronger research incentives can improve future productive capacity
Demand stabilization permanently raises technology by the same amount as spending, making research incentives unnecessary
ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9122.$correct: Demand stabilization can use idle capacity; stronger research incentives can improve future productive capacity
ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9122.feedback: Closing a demand gap and shifting the long-run productive frontier are different objectives. Research has a capacity channel and timing; a temporary demand boost is not a substitute for it.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9122.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Research incentives instantly eliminate every current demand shortfall without a timing lag” in this economic growth policy task.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9123.q: Firms underinvest in training because employees may leave with their new skills. Which proposal targets that mechanism while recognizing a resource tradeoff?
options: Subsidize current consumption; treat the resulting spending as equivalent to transferable training.
Co-finance transferable training; compare spillover benefits with the funds' alternative uses.
Protect current jobs from new technology; treat lower mobility as increased skill formation.
Raise the nominal GDP target; treat its dollar increase as additional human capital.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9123.$correct: Co-finance transferable training; compare spillover benefits with the funds' alternative uses.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9123.feedback: Training can create spillovers that private firms do not fully capture. Co-financing may address that incentive, but training uses resources and its social return must justify the cost.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARYBOSS-9123.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Mandate a higher nominal GDP target and infer that skills must improve” in this economic growth policy task.

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3027.q: An economy raises saving to finance new capital but temporarily consumes less. Under diminishing returns with unchanged technology, which comparison is defensible?
options: Current consumption rises; future output can rise; saving immediately releases resources for both uses.
Current consumption falls; future output must fall; diminishing returns mean negative capital contributions.
Current consumption falls; future output can rise; permanent faster growth needs more than capital deepening.
Current consumption falls; future output rises; capital deepening alone sustains permanently faster growth.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3027.$correct: Current consumption falls; future output can rise; permanent faster growth needs more than capital deepening.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3027.feedback: Saving reallocates resources from present consumption toward investment. Capital deepening can raise the level of output per worker, with diminishing increments absent continuing technological progress.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3027.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Higher saving permanently raises growth at an unchanged rate for every additional machine” in this economic growth policy task.

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3028.q: A region has reliable electricity but weak contract enforcement and frequent asset seizure. Which growth policy most directly addresses the stated binding constraint?
options: Add spare electricity capacity to eliminate the risk of seized investment returns.
Improve property and contract enforcement to reduce the risk of lost investment returns.
Protect existing firms from entry to substitute incumbent rents for enforceable contracts.
Raise nominal wages by decree to substitute higher money earnings for productive capacity.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3028.$correct: Improve property and contract enforcement to reduce the risk of lost investment returns.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3028.feedback: The stated constraint is insecurity of returns, not an electricity shortage. Predictable institutions can encourage investment and exchange; nominal changes alone do not establish real productivity gains.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3028.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Restrict all new firms to preserve incumbent returns and infer faster innovation” in this economic growth policy task.

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3029.q: A technology policy raises potential output for 140 workers but displaces some workers whose skills no longer match vacancies. Which package recognizes both the growth benefit and transition cost?
options: Support productive innovation and targeted retraining; higher potential output does not instantly rematch displaced workers
Stop measuring displaced workers so productivity and employment both improve by definition
Use only demand stimulus and assume it reverses every permanent skill change
Block every productivity improvement because any displacement proves long-run output must fall
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3029.$correct: Support productive innovation and targeted retraining; higher potential output does not instantly rematch displaced workers
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3029.feedback: Innovation can expand productive capacity while creating structural transition costs. Retraining/mobility address the mismatch; aggregate growth alone does not guarantee immediate employment for each displaced worker.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3029.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Stop measuring displaced workers so productivity and employment both improve by definition” in this economic growth policy task.

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3030.q: A research subsidy raises future productive capacity, but private spending is too weak to use existing capacity today. Which claim confuses the policy's time horizon?
options: That better research incentives alone necessarily close today's demand gap.
That research can affect future production methods and productive capacity.
That weak current spending can coexist with useful long-run investment opportunities.
That current stabilization and future productivity policy address different constraints.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3030.$correct: That better research incentives alone necessarily close today's demand gap.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3030.feedback: Research incentives can improve the long-run production frontier, but that does not establish an immediate increase in spending sufficient to close an existing recessionary gap. Demand utilization and productive capacity require separate diagnoses.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3030.commonError: Incorrect inference: That research can affect future production methods and productive capacity.

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3031.q: A training subsidy is justified by skills that benefit future employers. Evidence shows the subsidized course teaches only a proprietary process unusable elsewhere. Which part of the original case weakens?
options: The private-benefit rationale disappears; proprietary skills cannot improve any firm's output.
The resource cost disappears; training limited to one employer uses no scarce inputs.
The external-benefit rationale strengthens automatically; less transferability means larger spillovers.
The external-benefit rationale weakens; most benefits may remain with the current employer.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3031.$correct: The external-benefit rationale weakens; most benefits may remain with the current employer.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3031.feedback: The original subsidy rationale concerned benefits firms could not capture because skills were transferable. Firm-specific training weakens that particular externality argument, even though training can still have private value and resource costs.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3031.commonError: Incorrect inference: The private-benefit rationale disappears; proprietary skills cannot improve any firm's output.

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3032.q: Saving rises and capital per worker grows, but each extra unit of capital adds less output under unchanged technology. A forecast extends the initial output-growth increase forever. Which correction is warranted?
options: Total output must decline immediately; diminishing marginal returns mean negative capital productivity.
Current consumption must rise immediately; higher saving creates resources without an opportunity cost.
Transition growth can slow as marginal returns diminish; permanently faster growth needs another sustained source.
Transition growth must accelerate; diminishing returns make each later unit more productive.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3032.$correct: Transition growth can slow as marginal returns diminish; permanently faster growth needs another sustained source.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3032.feedback: Capital deepening can increase the output level and speed growth during transition, while diminishing marginal returns reduce successive gains. It does not alone establish a permanently higher growth rate under unchanged technology.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3032.commonError: Incorrect inference: Transition growth must accelerate; diminishing returns make each later unit more productive.

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3033.q: Reliable contract enforcement is established, but frequent electricity outages leave equipment idle. A proposal spends the entire growth budget on duplicating the legal reform. Which diagnosis challenges its priority?
options: More nominal spending alone supplies power; identifying the infrastructure bottleneck is unnecessary.
Power reliability is now the stated constraint; another legal reform does not directly operate idle equipment.
Contract enforcement is still necessarily the sole constraint; physical infrastructure cannot affect output.
Idle equipment proves labor skills are irrelevant; no policy can raise its productive use.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3033.$correct: Power reliability is now the stated constraint; another legal reform does not directly operate idle equipment.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3033.feedback: The binding constraint is context-dependent. With enforcement already reliable and outages idling machines, improving electricity availability addresses the specified barrier more directly than duplicating the legal reform.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3033.commonError: Incorrect inference: Contract enforcement is still necessarily the sole constraint; physical infrastructure cannot affect output.

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3034.q: A technology policy raises potential output for 190 workers but displaces some workers whose skills no longer match vacancies. Which package recognizes both the growth benefit and transition cost?
options: Support productive innovation and targeted retraining; higher potential output does not instantly rematch displaced workers

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3034.$correct: Support productive innovation and targeted retraining; higher potential output does not instantly rematch displaced workers
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3034.feedback: Innovation can expand productive capacity while creating structural transition costs. Retraining/mobility address the mismatch; aggregate growth alone does not guarantee immediate employment for each displaced worker.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3034.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Stop measuring displaced workers so productivity and employment both improve by definition” in this economic growth policy task.

ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3035.q: An economy is already at potential output but has weak incentives for innovation. Officials propose sustained demand stimulus as their only growth strategy. Which comparison is appropriate?
options: Stronger demand permanently raises capacity; innovation incentives affect only current prices.
Both policies affect only current prices; productive capacity cannot respond to innovation.
Both policies permanently raise capacity equally; higher nominal spending is real growth.
Stronger demand mainly pressures current prices; better innovation incentives can expand future capacity.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3035.$correct: Stronger demand mainly pressures current prices; better innovation incentives can expand future capacity.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3035.feedback: At potential, sustained demand expansion does not by itself supply more technology or resources. Innovation policy addresses a real source of future productive capacity, subject to its costs and effectiveness.
ECON-NL-MEDIUMBOSS-3035.commonError: Incorrect inference: Stronger demand permanently raises capacity; innovation incentives affect only current prices.

PM2B3-POL-EB-001.q: Workers can borrow affordably for transferable training and keep its full future earnings benefit. No spillover to others is identified. Does transferability alone establish a subsidy case?
options: Yes; affordable borrowing means training has no opportunity cost for society.
No; privately financed skills cannot contribute to workers' productivity or earnings.
No; the stated financing and benefit assumptions remove the proposed market-failure rationale.
Yes; every transferable skill creates an external benefit equal to its private return.
PM2B3-POL-EB-001.$correct: No; the stated financing and benefit assumptions remove the proposed market-failure rationale.
PM2B3-POL-EB-001.feedback: Transferability alone is not an externality. If trainees can finance training and capture its benefits, the stated case supplies neither a credit constraint nor an unpriced benefit; another justification would need evidence.
PM2B3-POL-EB-001.commonError: Incorrect inference: Yes; every transferable skill creates an external benefit equal to its private return.

PM2B3-POL-EB-002.q: A saving policy sacrifices current consumption for a higher future output level. A second proposal achieves the same future output with less current sacrifice. Which comparison bears on choosing between them?
options: Neither can raise future output; consuming less rules out producing additional capital.
The second has a lower stated transition cost; timing and other costs still need comparison.
Both have identical welfare effects; equal future output rules out any importance of current consumption.
The first is superior by definition; a larger saving sacrifice proves a larger future benefit.
PM2B3-POL-EB-002.$correct: The second has a lower stated transition cost; timing and other costs still need comparison.
PM2B3-POL-EB-002.feedback: Equal future output does not make transition costs irrelevant. Less current consumption sacrifice is an advantage on the stated margin, while a complete choice also considers timing, risk and any omitted costs or benefits.
PM2B3-POL-EB-002.commonError: Incorrect inference: Both have identical welfare effects; equal future output rules out any importance of current consumption.

PM2B3-POL-EB-003.q: A property-rights reform improves investors' expected returns, but a shortage of trained workers prevents new machines from operating. Which inference limits a forecast of immediate catch-up?
options: Better incentives can induce investment, but complementary skills still constrain realized production.
Better incentives automatically supply skilled workers; the stated shortage cannot affect output.
The shortage proves enforcement did not improve; incentives and skills measure the same thing.
The reform lowers productive capacity; higher expected returns reduce the use of machinery.
PM2B3-POL-EB-003.$correct: Better incentives can induce investment, but complementary skills still constrain realized production.
PM2B3-POL-EB-003.feedback: Secure returns can encourage investment without providing every complementary input. A skill bottleneck can delay production benefits even when the institutional reform works on its intended incentive margin.
PM2B3-POL-EB-003.commonError: Incorrect inference: Better incentives automatically supply skilled workers; the stated shortage cannot affect output.

PM2B3-POL-FB-004.q: A technology policy raises potential output for 240 workers but displaces some workers whose skills no longer match vacancies. Which package recognizes both the growth benefit and transition cost?
options: Use only demand stimulus and assume it reverses every permanent skill change
Block every productivity improvement because any displacement proves long-run output must fall

Stop measuring displaced workers so productivity and employment both improve by definition
PM2B3-POL-FB-004.$correct: Support productive innovation and targeted retraining; higher potential output does not instantly rematch displaced workers

PM2B3-POL-FB-004.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Use only demand stimulus and assume it reverses every permanent skill change” in this economic growth policy task.

PM2B3-POL-FB-005.q: A government must choose between accelerating a useful research program and temporary purchases during a demand slump. Does the slump prove the research program has no value?

No; current stabilization and future capacity benefits are different margins in allocating scarce resources.
Yes; idle capacity makes every investment in future technology economically worthless.
No; research spending automatically eliminates the current output gap without a demand calculation.
PM2B3-POL-FB-005.$correct: No; current stabilization and future capacity benefits are different margins in allocating scarce resources.

LG-Q-2000.q: A customer deposits $100 of currency into checking. A bank later makes a separate loan by crediting a borrower's checking account. Which comparison correctly separates the two events?

Both events create new M1 equal to the amounts credited because checking balances rise
Neither event can change M1 because every bank deposit merely replaces currency
The currency deposit creates new M1; lending changes only the ownership of existing currency
LG-Q-2000.$correct: The currency deposit changes M1 composition; the later loan can create a new deposit and raise M1
LG-Q-2000.feedback: In the first event, public currency falls as checking rises; in the second, a loan asset and deposit liability are created together. The initial transfer and subsequent credit creation must not be conflated.
LG-Q-2000.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both events create new M1 equal to the amounts credited because checking balances rise” in this money functions and measures task.

LG-Q-2002.q: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. Currency is $900, checking $1,100, savings $1,500 and small time deposits $500. A household moves $400 from checking to savings. Which final totals and interpretation are correct?

M1: $1,600; M2: $3,600; the transfer removes funds from both aggregates.
M1: $1,600; M2: $4,000; historical narrow money falls, broad money is unchanged.
M1: $2,000; M2: $4,000; the transfer changes neither historical monetary aggregate.

LG-Q-2002.commonError: Incorrect inference: M1: $3,500; M2: $4,000; savings were already counted in historical narrow money.

P52B-S3-MFM-B2-001.q: A store quotes a $140 price in dollars but accepts a card that transfers dollars from a deposit account. A student calls the card a fourth function of money. Which correction connects the instrument and functions?

P52B-S3-MFM-B2-001.commonError: Incorrect inference: Quote: store of value; deposit: transfer instrument; card: unit of account.

P52B-S3-MFM-B2-002.q: A report lists currency $160, checking $320, savings $480, and small time deposits $160. It adds savings to an M1 total that already includes savings. Using current U.S. definitions, which corrected pair avoids double counting?
P52B-S3-MFM-B2-002.feedback: M1 = 160+320+480 = 960. M2 adds the time deposit once: 960+160 = 1120. Savings already inside M1 must not be added again.
P52B-S3-MFM-B2-002.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “M1 = $960; M2 = $1600” in this money functions and measures task.

P52B-S3-MFM-B2-003.q: A customer deposits $180 of currency into checking. A bank later makes a separate loan by crediting a borrower's checking account. Which comparison correctly separates the two events?

The currency deposit changes M1 composition; the later loan can create a new deposit and raise M1
Both events create new M1 equal to the amounts credited because checking balances rise

P52B-S3-MFM-B2-003.feedback: In the first event, public currency falls as checking rises; in the second, a loan asset and deposit liability are created together. The initial transfer and subsequent credit creation must not be conflated.

P52B-S3-MFM-B3-001.q: A household holds $200 in checking, $400 in savings, and $200 in a small time deposit. Under current U.S. definitions, it transfers the time deposit into savings. Which M1/M2 changes follow?

Both M1 and M2 rise $200
M1 falls $200; M2 is unchanged
M1 rises $200; M2 is unchanged
P52B-S3-MFM-B3-001.feedback: Current M1 includes savings but not small time deposits. The transfer moves funds into M1 while remaining inside M2, so it is a reclassification within broad money, not an M2 increase.
P52B-S3-MFM-B3-001.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “M1 is unchanged; M2 rises $200” in this money functions and measures task.

Temporary liquidity can bridge the first bank's timing gap; lending alone does not erase the second bank's capital loss
Both banks become solvent whenever a central bank supplies reserves, regardless of asset values

LG-Q-2003.$correct: Temporary liquidity can bridge the first bank's timing gap; lending alone does not erase the second bank's capital loss

LG-Q-2003.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The first bank needs only a fiscal tax cut; the second needs only a new deposit classification” in this central bank and federal reserve task.

Fiscal authorities authorize spending; the central bank implements monetary policy under its legal mandate and accountability framework

LG-Q-2005.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The central bank writes the spending appropriation whenever monetary policy is independent” in this central bank and federal reserve task.

LG-Q-9111.$correct: Reserves rise; lending still depends on demand, risk and capital.
LG-Q-9111.feedback: Reserves are central-bank liabilities held by banks. Commercial lending creates bank assets and deposits and depends on additional constraints; reserves alone do not compel lending or create equity.
LG-Q-9111.commonError: Incorrect inference: Reserves stay fixed; weak loan demand prevents central-bank reserve creation.

LG-Q-2007.q: A bank has deposits $1000, reserves $200, and a required reserve ratio of 10% in a simplified model. A depositor withdraws $100 in currency. Assume no other balance-sheet change. Which reserve diagnosis follows?
options: Reserves become $100, required reserves become $110, and there is a $10 shortfall
Reserves become $100, required reserves $90, and excess reserves $10
Reserves become $100, required reserves remain $100, and excess reserves are zero
Reserves stay $200, required reserves become $90, and excess reserves $110
LG-Q-2007.$correct: Reserves become $100, required reserves $90, and excess reserves $10
LG-Q-2007.feedback: The cash withdrawal reduces deposits and reserves by 100. Required reserves are 10% of 900 = 90; actual reserves 100 leave 10 excess. Both sides of the reserve calculation must reflect the withdrawal.
LG-Q-2007.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Reserves become $100, required reserves become $110, and there is a $10 shortfall” in this bank balance sheets reserves and capital task.

LG-Q-9104.q: A bank has assets $1440, deposit liabilities $1200 and capital $240. Loan losses reduce assets by $360; liabilities do not fall. Which remedy addresses the resulting problem?
options: Capital: −$120; new equity addresses insolvency, a liquidity loan alone does not.
Capital: +$240; loan losses affect liquidity rather than the owners' residual claim.
Capital: +$600; writing off loans reduces deposit liabilities rather than bank assets.
Capital: $0 after borrowing $120; the loan raises assets without matching liabilities.
LG-Q-9104.$correct: Capital: −$120; new equity addresses insolvency, a liquidity loan alone does not.
LG-Q-9104.feedback: After losses, assets are 1080 and liabilities 1200; capital is −120. Borrowed liquidity raises assets and liabilities equally, leaving net worth unchanged.
LG-Q-9104.commonError: Incorrect inference: Capital: +$240; loan losses affect liquidity rather than the owners' residual claim.

LG-Q-9105.q: A bank grants a $140 loan by crediting the borrower's checking account; no cash leaves initially. Which entries and subsequent constraint are correct?
options: Reserve assets and capital each rise $140; no deposit liability is created
Deposit liabilities fall $140 while loan assets rise; the bank's net worth rises immediately
The bank must first reduce another customer's deposit by $140; total deposits cannot increase
Loan assets and deposit liabilities each rise $140; later payments may require reserve settlement
LG-Q-9105.$correct: Loan assets and deposit liabilities each rise $140; later payments may require reserve settlement
LG-Q-9105.feedback: Loan origination creates a bank asset and a matching deposit liability, not instant bank equity. If the deposit is spent to another bank, settlement can create a reserve need.
LG-Q-9105.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Reserve assets and capital each rise $140; no deposit liability is created” in this bank balance sheets reserves and capital task.

P52A-BANK-B2-001.q: A bank has reserves $320 and deposits $1600; the simplified required reserve ratio is 10%. Management says it can lend all $320 without acquiring reserves. Which correction is justified before considering capital and credit risk?
options: Only $160 is initially excess reserves; the $160 required portion must remain against existing deposits
All $320 is excess because required reserves are calculated only after lending
No reserves are excess because every reserve dollar is bank capital
It can lend $3200 immediately from its own reserves because the system multiplier applies to one bank's first loan
P52A-BANK-B2-001.$correct: Only $160 is initially excess reserves; the $160 required portion must remain against existing deposits
P52A-BANK-B2-001.feedback: Required reserves are .10×1600 = 160; excess is 320−160 = 160. A single bank's immediate capacity is distinct from a system-wide redepositing maximum.
P52A-BANK-B2-001.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “All $320 is excess because required reserves are calculated only after lending” in this bank balance sheets reserves and capital task.
