LG-Q-2006.q: In a simplified system with a 20% reserve ratio, no currency leakage and no excess reserves, $100 of new reserves enters. A student calls the first bank's $80 initial loan the system's total deposit increase. Which correction is correct?
options: The maximum total deposit increase is $100; banks cannot create deposits by lending
The maximum total deposit increase is $600; add the original reserve injection to the multiplier result again
The maximum total deposit increase is $500; repeated lending and redepositing extends beyond the first loan
The maximum total deposit increase is $80; later deposits are excluded from money
LG-Q-2006.$correct: The maximum total deposit increase is $500; repeated lending and redepositing extends beyond the first loan
LG-Q-2006.feedback: The simple maximum is ΔR/rr = 100/.20 = 500. The first-round loan is not the total expansion; the multiplier result already includes the deposits supported by the initial reserves.
LG-Q-2006.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The maximum total deposit increase is $100; banks cannot create deposits by lending” in this deposit creation and money multiplier task.

LG-Q-2008.q: The public deposits $120 of previously held currency in a system with rr=10%, no later currency leakage and no excess reserves. At the simple maximum, how does total deposit expansion compare with the net increase in M1?

Deposits and net M1 both rise $1200; ignore the reduction in public currency
Deposits rise $1080 while net M1 rises $1200; subtract the currency from deposits only
Deposits and net M1 both rise $120; all subsequent loans transfer existing deposits only
LG-Q-2008.$correct: Deposits can rise $1200, while net M1 rises $1080 because public currency initially falls $120
LG-Q-2008.feedback: The deposit maximum is 120/.1 = 1200. M1 includes public currency, which falls 120; net M1 change is 1200−120 = 1080. Deposit growth and net new money differ for an initial currency deposit.
LG-Q-2008.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Deposits and net M1 both rise $1200; ignore the reduction in public currency” in this deposit creation and money multiplier task.

LG-Q-9102.q: New reserves of $140 arrive. A 10% required ratio suggests a simple multiplier of 10, but banks also hold reserves equal to 10% of deposits; assume no currency leakage. Which maximum uses both reserve needs?

$700 in total deposits; the effective reserve fraction is 20%
$1400 in total deposits; excess reserves never constrain lending

LG-Q-9102.feedback: Required plus additional reserves total 20% of deposits. Thus deposits supported by 140 new reserves are 140/.20 = 700, rather than the required-ratio-only maximum.
LG-Q-9102.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “$2800 in total deposits; add the reciprocals of the two ratios” in this deposit creation and money multiplier task.

LG-Q-9109.q: A textbook system has rr=25%, no currency leakage and no excess reserves. Policy removes $160 in reserves. Which statement combines the direction and meaning of the model's maximum adjustment?

LG-Q-2012.q: A simplified rr=10% model predicts a $1000 deposit maximum from $100 in new reserves. Actual deposits rise only $400. Which diagnosis and inference are justified?

Reserve hoarding or currency leakage can lower the expansion; the effective multiplier here is 4
The required ratio must be 25%; behavior can never lower expansion below the reciprocal rule
The banks must have created negative reserves because every prediction is an accounting identity
LG-Q-2012.$correct: Reserve hoarding or currency leakage can lower the expansion; the effective multiplier here is 4

LG-Q-2012.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The shortfall proves the central bank cannot create reserves in the first place” in this monetary control limits task.

Loans require equal reductions in existing deposits; weak demand preserves deposits.
LG-Q-2013.$correct: Banks need willing, qualified borrowers as well as reserve capacity.
LG-Q-2013.feedback: Having liquidity is different from finding loans acceptable to both lender and borrower. Reserve supply alone does not establish demand, risk-adjusted profitability or capital headroom.
LG-Q-2013.commonError: Incorrect inference: Reserve creation requires prior loan applications; weak demand prevents the injection.

43071.q: In a simplified closed-economy account, net taxes are $100 and government purchases $120. A new policy raises both by $20. Which conclusion separates the budget position from the balanced policy change?
options: Public saving becomes +$20; the larger tax total makes the initial deficit irrelevant
Public saving remains −$20; equal changes leave the initial deficit unchanged
Public saving becomes zero; any equal tax-and-spending change balances the whole budget
Public saving becomes −$40; count higher purchases but ignore higher net taxes
43071.$correct: Public saving remains −$20; equal changes leave the initial deficit unchanged
43071.feedback: Before: T−G=100−120=−20. After: 120−140=−20. Equal changes do not erase the initial imbalance.
43071.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Public saving becomes +$20; the larger tax total makes the initial deficit irrelevant” in this budget accounting and public saving task.

43072.q: Government receives $180 in taxes, pays $30 in transfers and buys $150 of current output. Define net taxes as taxes minus transfers. A report calls the transfers an additional purchase. Which accounts are consistent?

Net taxes are $180, purchases $180, public saving zero; transfers are G
Net taxes are $150, purchases $180, public saving −$30; count transfers twice
Net taxes are $180, purchases $150, public saving +$30; ignore transfers in the budget
43072.$correct: Net taxes are $150, purchases $150, public saving zero; transfers are not G
43072.feedback: Transfers reduce net taxes in this convention and are not purchases of current output. Tnet−G = (gross taxes−transfers)−purchases = 0.
43072.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Net taxes are $180, purchases $180, public saving zero; transfers are G” in this budget accounting and public saving task.

LG-Q-3000.q: Money is initially $100, velocity 4 and real output 200. Money rises 10%, velocity falls 10%, and real output is unchanged. Which conclusion corrects the claim that prices must rise 10%?
options: The price level rises 10%; money growth alone determines prices without a velocity assumption
The price level is unchanged; equal opposite percentage changes exactly cancel
The price level falls 10%; ignore the simultaneous money increase
The price level falls 1%; the opposing percentage changes in M and V combine multiplicatively
LG-Q-3000.$correct: The price level falls 1%; the opposing percentage changes in M and V combine multiplicatively
LG-Q-3000.feedback: MV=PY. With Y fixed, P changes by the product of M and V factors: 1.10×0.90=.99, a 1% fall. A constant-velocity shortcut is not valid here.
LG-Q-3000.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The price level rises 10%; money growth alone determines prices without a velocity assumption” in this quantity theory of money task.

LG-Q-3001.q: Money is $120, velocity is 5, and the price level is 2. A report gives real output as 600. Which corrected output and interpretation are consistent with MV=PY?

Real output is 300; 600 is nominal spending, which must be divided by the price level
Real output is 1200; multiply nominal spending by the price level
LG-Q-3001.$correct: Real output is 300; 600 is nominal spending, which must be divided by the price level
LG-Q-3001.feedback: MV=120×5=600, a nominal-spending measure. Real output is MV/P=600/2=300.
LG-Q-3001.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Real output is 600; the price level does not enter real output” in this quantity theory of money task.

LG-Q-3002.feedback: The exact price factor is 1.05×1/1.05=1. Money growth alone cannot determine inflation when real output changes too.
LG-Q-3002.commonError: Incorrect inference: Prices rise 5%; money growth determines inflation without adjusting for output.

About 4.0% money growth; falling velocity amplifies the desired spending increase

P52B-S4-QTM-B1-003.$correct: Real output is 700; 1400 is nominal spending, which must be divided by the price level
P52B-S4-QTM-B1-003.feedback: MV=280×5=1400, a nominal-spending measure. Real output is MV/P=1400/2=700.
P52B-S4-QTM-B1-003.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Real output is 2800; multiply nominal spending by the price level” in this quantity theory of money task.

P52B-S4-QTM-B3-001.q: Nominal spending rises 10% while real output rises 10%. A proposal treats the spending increase as a 10% rise in prices. Which quantity-equation comparison corrects it?
options: The price level is unchanged; nominal spending and real output rose by the same factor.
The price level rises 20%; add the spending and output growth rates.
The price level rises 10%; output growth does not enter the spending identity.
The price level falls 10%; output growth alone determines the price-level change.
P52B-S4-QTM-B3-001.$correct: The price level is unchanged; nominal spending and real output rose by the same factor.
P52B-S4-QTM-B3-001.feedback: P=MV/Y. When nominal spending MV and real output Y both rise by 1.10, their ratio and therefore P are unchanged. Nominal spending growth is not itself the inflation rate.
P52B-S4-QTM-B3-001.commonError: Incorrect inference: The price level rises 20%; add the spending and output growth rates.

P52B-S4-QTM-B3-002.q: A country has nominal spending $1280. It aims for a 3% price-level increase with real output up 2% and velocity down 1%. What money-growth factor is required, and why is adding 3% and 2% incomplete?
options: Exactly 5% money growth; velocity does not affect the target
About 4.0% money growth; falling velocity amplifies the desired spending increase
Exactly 1% money growth; subtract real growth from the price target
About 6.1% money growth; falling velocity also has to be offset
P52B-S4-QTM-B3-002.$correct: About 6.1% money growth; falling velocity also has to be offset
P52B-S4-QTM-B3-002.feedback: Solve M factor = P factor × Y factor / V factor = 1.03×1.02/.99≈1.06121, or 6.1%. The velocity decline reduces spending per dollar and requires additional money growth.
P52B-S4-QTM-B3-002.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Exactly 5% money growth; velocity does not affect the target” in this quantity theory of money task.

P52B-S4-QTM-B3-003.q: Money is initially $340, velocity 4 and real output 680. Money rises 10%, velocity falls 10%, and real output is unchanged. Which conclusion corrects the claim that prices must rise 10%?
options: The price level is unchanged; equal opposite percentage changes exactly cancel
The price level falls 10%; ignore the simultaneous money increase
The price level falls 1%; the opposing percentage changes in M and V combine multiplicatively
The price level rises 10%; money growth alone determines prices without a velocity assumption
P52B-S4-QTM-B3-003.$correct: The price level falls 1%; the opposing percentage changes in M and V combine multiplicatively
P52B-S4-QTM-B3-003.feedback: MV=PY. With Y fixed, P changes by the product of M and V factors: 1.10×0.90=.99, a 1% fall. A constant-velocity shortcut is not valid here.
P52B-S4-QTM-B3-003.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The price level is unchanged; equal opposite percentage changes exactly cancel” in this quantity theory of money task.

LG-Q-3003.q: A worker initially earns $100 while the consumption-price index is 100. In a long-run monetary-neutrality comparison, nominal wages and all prices double while real technology and resources are unchanged. Which conclusion respects both nominal and real measures?
options: Nominal pay doubles while the real wage and long-run productive capacity can remain unchanged
The real wage doubles because its numerator doubles, even though prices also double
Productive capacity doubles because a larger money stock is itself more real capital
Nominal pay is unchanged because neutrality freezes every monetary variable
LG-Q-3003.$correct: Nominal pay doubles while the real wage and long-run productive capacity can remain unchanged
LG-Q-3003.feedback: A real wage is nominal wage divided by prices; doubling both preserves the ratio. Long-run neutrality permits nominal changes without corresponding changes in real productive capacity.
LG-Q-3003.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The real wage doubles because its numerator doubles, even though prices also double” in this monetary neutrality task.

LG-Q-3004.q: A one-time increase in money causes temporary output above potential. Over time wages and expected prices adjust. Which comparison avoids confusing long-run neutrality with immediate neutrality?
options: Short-run output stays at potential; long-run neutrality also rules out temporary real effects.
Short-run output rises; long-run potential rises equally despite unchanged productive resources.
Short-run output rises; long-run neutrality requires prices to return to their original level.
Short-run output can rise; long-run output returns to potential at higher prices.
LG-Q-3004.$correct: Short-run output can rise; long-run output returns to potential at higher prices.
LG-Q-3004.feedback: Sticky wages/prices allow short-run real effects. Longer-run adjustment can return output to potential while nominal prices stay higher; neutrality does not require no transitional effect.
LG-Q-3004.commonError: Incorrect inference: Short-run output stays at potential; long-run neutrality also rules out temporary real effects.

LG-Q-3005.q: Nominal wages rise 6%, while prices rise 4%. A claim that these changes demonstrate complete monetary neutrality is made. Which assessment follows from the real-wage evidence?
options: The real wage rises 10%; nominal wage and price growth should be added
The real wage falls about 1.9%; the price factor belongs in the numerator
The real wage rises about 1.9%; these unequal proportional changes do not by themselves demonstrate unchanged real wages
The real wage is unchanged because any simultaneous nominal wage and price rise is neutral
LG-Q-3005.$correct: The real wage rises about 1.9%; these unequal proportional changes do not by themselves demonstrate unchanged real wages
LG-Q-3005.feedback: The real-wage factor is 1.06/1.04≈1.01923. Equal proportional nominal changes would leave the ratio unchanged; these are not equal. The calculation alone also does not identify what caused the changes.
LG-Q-3005.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The real wage rises 10%; nominal wage and price growth should be added” in this monetary neutrality task.

LG-Q-9123.q: Money growth rises permanently in an economy whose real productive resources remain 160 index units. Under the stated long-run quantity-theory/neutrality assumptions with stable velocity, which distinction is correct?
options: Faster money growth and a one-time increase both raise sustained inflation equally.
Faster money growth raises sustained real growth; a one-time increase raises real capacity.
Faster money growth and a one-time increase leave both nominal price measures unchanged.
Faster money growth raises sustained inflation; a one-time increase raises the price level.
LG-Q-9123.$correct: Faster money growth raises sustained inflation; a one-time increase raises the price level.
LG-Q-9123.feedback: Levels and growth rates differ: a lasting growth-rate change can sustain inflation, whereas a one-time level change is not ongoing faster money growth. Real capacity remains determined by the stated real factors.
LG-Q-9123.commonError: Incorrect inference: Faster money growth and a one-time increase both raise sustained inflation equally.

That proportional nominal adjustments can leave relative prices unchanged

That temporary real effects can coexist with an unchanged long-run level

PM2C2-NEUT-EB-003.q: Nominal wages and the price level both rise 6%. A report concludes that every real variable was unchanged. Which inference is supported and which is too broad?
options: Real wages rise 6%; that establishes unchanged employment and output.
Real wages fall 6%; that establishes lower productive capacity in the long run.
Real wages rise 12%; that proves complete monetary neutrality across real variables.
Real wages are unchanged; that alone does not establish unchanged employment or output.

LG-Q-3006.q: For a $100 loan, expected inflation rises from 2% to 5% while the required expected real return falls from 4% to 3%. Under the Fisher approximation, which nominal-rate comparison is correct?
options: The nominal rate remains 6%; opposite movements in components must cancel exactly
The nominal rate rises from 6% to 8%; the real-rate decline partly offsets the inflation-expectation increase
The nominal rate rises from 6% to 9%; the real rate must be held fixed despite the supplied change
The nominal rate falls from 6% to 5%; subtract expected inflation from the required real return
LG-Q-3006.$correct: The nominal rate rises from 6% to 8%; the real-rate decline partly offsets the inflation-expectation increase
LG-Q-3006.feedback: Initially i≈r+πe=4+2=6. Later i≈3+5=8. A one-for-one response to expected inflation requires a fixed real rate, which is not the case here.
LG-Q-3006.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The nominal rate remains 6%; opposite movements in components must cancel exactly” in this fisher effect task.

LG-Q-3007.q: A $120 fixed-rate loan has nominal interest 7% when expected inflation is 3%. Actual inflation later turns out to be 6%. Which pair separates the rate-setting prediction from the realized outcome?
options: The expected real return was about 4%; the realized real return is about 1%, without changing the signed nominal rate
The expected real return was about 1%; the nominal contract automatically resets to 10% after inflation is observed
Both expected and realized real returns are 4% because the lender chose a fixed nominal rate
The nominal rate becomes 6% because actual inflation replaces the contractual rate
LG-Q-3007.$correct: The expected real return was about 4%; the realized real return is about 1%, without changing the signed nominal rate
LG-Q-3007.feedback: Fisher rate setting uses expected inflation at agreement; ex post purchasing power uses actual inflation. Thus 7−3=4% expected and 7−6=1% realized; the nominal contract remains 7%.
LG-Q-3007.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The expected real return was about 1%; the nominal contract automatically resets to 10% after inflation is observed” in this fisher effect task.

LG-Q-3008.q: In a loan market financing $140 of projects, nominal rates fall 2 percentage points while the expected real rate is unchanged. Within the Fisher approximation, what inference follows and what remains unproved?
options: Expected inflation rose 2 points; actual future inflation must rise equally
Actual inflation already fell 2 points; no expectation assumption is needed
The real rate fell 2 points despite the stated fixed-real-rate condition
Expected inflation fell 2 points; actual future inflation need not equal that forecast
LG-Q-3008.$correct: Expected inflation fell 2 points; actual future inflation need not equal that forecast
LG-Q-3008.feedback: With Δr=0, Δi≈Δπe. A two-point nominal decline implies a two-point expectation decline in this model, but forecasts are not necessarily realized.
LG-Q-3008.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Expected inflation rose 2 points; actual future inflation must rise equally” in this fisher effect task.

LG-Q-9117.q: Expected inflation rises 4 points in a credit market of size $160, but the nominal rate rises only 1 point. If the Fisher approximation applies, which reconciliation is correct?
options: The expected real rate fell 3 points; a changing real rate explains the less-than-one-for-one nominal response
The expected real rate rose 3 points; subtract the nominal change from inflation expectations
The approximation proves the data impossible because the real rate cannot change
The actual inflation rate must have fallen 3 points because expected and actual inflation are interchangeable
LG-Q-9117.$correct: The expected real rate fell 3 points; a changing real rate explains the less-than-one-for-one nominal response
LG-Q-9117.feedback: Δi=Δr+Δπe implies Δr=1−4=−3 points. A changing real component is compatible with the identity; actual inflation is a separate outcome.
LG-Q-9117.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The expected real rate rose 3 points; subtract the nominal change from inflation expectations” in this fisher effect task.

LG-Q-3009.q: A firm spends $100 repeatedly updating posted prices, and households make extra account transfers to avoid idle cash. Inflation is perfectly anticipated. Which comparison identifies costs that need not disappear with correct forecasts?

Borrower and lender redistribution, respectively; both disappear with anticipated inflation.
Menu and shoeleather costs, respectively; both can persist with anticipated inflation.
Pure nominal changes in both cases; neither uses real resources with anticipated inflation.
LG-Q-3009.$correct: Menu and shoeleather costs, respectively; both can persist with anticipated inflation.
LG-Q-3009.feedback: Menu and shoeleather costs concern resources spent adapting to inflation. Correct forecasts can reduce unexpected contract redistribution without eliminating these costs.
LG-Q-3009.commonError: Incorrect inference: Shoeleather and menu costs, respectively; both can persist with anticipated inflation.

LG-Q-3010.q: A $120 fixed nominal debt was agreed with expected inflation 2%, but actual inflation is 7%. At the same time, firms incur real repricing costs. Which combined assessment is correct?
options: Borrower gains exactly equal a social resource gain, so repricing cannot reduce welfare
Repricing redistributes debt obligations but uses no real resources, so it is the same as surprise inflation
Unexpected inflation benefits the borrower relative to the lender, while repricing consumes real resources
Unexpected inflation benefits the lender relative to the borrower, while repricing consumes real resources
LG-Q-3010.$correct: Unexpected inflation benefits the borrower relative to the lender, while repricing consumes real resources
LG-Q-3010.feedback: A lower-than-expected real repayment transfers purchasing power toward borrowers. Repricing is a resource cost, so redistribution and efficiency costs are conceptually different.
LG-Q-3010.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Borrower gains exactly equal a social resource gain, so repricing cannot reduce welfare” in this inflation costs task.

LG-Q-3011.q: Two economies each have $140 in fixed nominal contracts. One unexpectedly raises inflation; the other credibly announces the same inflation before new contracts are written. Which difference is supported?
options: Both paths must have identical redistribution regardless of contract timing and indexation
The surprise creates more unexpected redistribution on existing contracts; the anticipated path can still create resource costs
The anticipated path must be economically costless because contracts can price every resource cost away
The surprise benefits all borrowers and lenders equally because the price level rises for both

LG-Q-3011.feedback: Contract timing and expectations determine surprise redistribution. Anticipation allows adjustment but does not generally remove repricing, cash-management or tax-distortion costs.
LG-Q-3011.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both paths must have identical redistribution regardless of contract timing and indexation” in this inflation costs task.

LG-Q-9119.q: Compare two $100 one-year loans using the Fisher approximation. Loan A fixes nominal interest at 10%; Loan B promises a 6% real return through full inflation indexation. Inflation was expected to be 4% but is 11%. Which realized lender return and redistribution comparison is correct?

A: 6%, B: 6%; expected inflation fixes both realized real returns.
A: −1%, B: 6%; only A's borrower gains from the inflation surprise.
A: 6%, B: −1%; only B's borrower gains from the inflation surprise.

LG-Q-9119.commonError: Incorrect inference: A: −1%, B: −1%; both borrowers gain equally from the inflation surprise.

options: Shoeleather and menu costs, respectively; both can persist with anticipated inflation.
Menu and shoeleather costs, respectively; both can persist with anticipated inflation.
Borrower and lender redistribution, respectively; both disappear with anticipated inflation.
Pure nominal changes in both cases; neither uses real resources with anticipated inflation.
PM2C2-ICOST-EB-003.$correct: Menu and shoeleather costs, respectively; both can persist with anticipated inflation.
PM2C2-ICOST-EB-003.feedback: Menu and shoeleather costs concern resources spent adapting to inflation. Correct forecasts can reduce unexpected contract redistribution without eliminating these costs.
PM2C2-ICOST-EB-003.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both are nominal changes with no possible use of real time or resources” in this inflation costs task.

PM2C2-ICOST-FB-004.q: A $280 fixed nominal debt was agreed with expected inflation 2%, but actual inflation is 7%. At the same time, firms incur real repricing costs. Which combined assessment is correct?
options: Unexpected inflation benefits the lender relative to the borrower, while repricing consumes real resources
Borrower gains exactly equal a social resource gain, so repricing cannot reduce welfare
Repricing redistributes debt obligations but uses no real resources, so it is the same as surprise inflation
Unexpected inflation benefits the borrower relative to the lender, while repricing consumes real resources
PM2C2-ICOST-FB-004.$correct: Unexpected inflation benefits the borrower relative to the lender, while repricing consumes real resources
PM2C2-ICOST-FB-004.feedback: A lower-than-expected real repayment transfers purchasing power toward borrowers. Repricing is a resource cost, so redistribution and efficiency costs are conceptually different.
PM2C2-ICOST-FB-004.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Unexpected inflation benefits the lender relative to the borrower, while repricing consumes real resources” in this inflation costs task.

PM2C2-ICOST-FB-005.q: Two economies each have $300 in fixed nominal contracts. One unexpectedly raises inflation; the other credibly announces the same inflation before new contracts are written. Which difference is supported?
options: The surprise benefits all borrowers and lenders equally because the price level rises for both
Both paths must have identical redistribution regardless of contract timing and indexation
The surprise creates more unexpected redistribution on existing contracts; the anticipated path can still create resource costs
The anticipated path must be economically costless because contracts can price every resource cost away
PM2C2-ICOST-FB-005.$correct: The surprise creates more unexpected redistribution on existing contracts; the anticipated path can still create resource costs
PM2C2-ICOST-FB-005.feedback: Contract timing and expectations determine surprise redistribution. Anticipation allows adjustment but does not generally remove repricing, cash-management or tax-distortion costs.
PM2C2-ICOST-FB-005.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The surprise benefits all borrowers and lenders equally because the price level rises for both” in this inflation costs task.

PM2C2-ICOST-FB-006.q: A saver earns a nominal $320 return that only compensates for inflation. The tax system taxes the entire nominal return without inflation adjustment. Which inference follows?
options: The nominal return is all a real gain because inflation compensation counts as extra purchasing power
Tax can reduce real principal despite a zero pre-tax real gain; nominal income and real income differ
No tax distortion is possible because a zero real gain implies a zero nominal tax base
The tax increases the saver's real return because it is charged in nominal dollars
PM2C2-ICOST-FB-006.$correct: Tax can reduce real principal despite a zero pre-tax real gain; nominal income and real income differ
PM2C2-ICOST-FB-006.feedback: A tax on nominal interest can tax inflation compensation as though it were real income. After-tax purchasing power can therefore fall even when the pre-tax real return is zero.
PM2C2-ICOST-FB-006.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The nominal return is all a real gain because inflation compensation counts as extra purchasing power” in this inflation costs task.

LG-Q-3012.q: A household holds $100 in currency while the price level rises 25%. No interest is paid. Which loss and interpretation fit the inflation-tax mechanism?
options: Real purchasing power falls 20%; nominal cash is unchanged without a tax bill.
Real purchasing power falls 25%; the price rise is the purchasing-power loss.
Nominal cash falls 25%; inflation removes currency through an implicit tax bill.
Real purchasing power is unchanged; holding the same nominal cash preserves its value.
LG-Q-3012.$correct: Real purchasing power falls 20%; nominal cash is unchanged without a tax bill.
LG-Q-3012.feedback: Real balances are M/P. With nominal currency fixed and prices multiplied by 1.25, purchasing power becomes 1/1.25=.8 of its original level, a 20% loss.
LG-Q-3012.commonError: Incorrect inference: Real purchasing power falls 25%; the price rise is the purchasing-power loss.

LG-Q-3013.q: Inflation falls from 8% to 3%. A report calls this a fall in the price level and predicts a lower real burden of fixed nominal debt. Which correction is needed?
options: Deflation: prices fall 5%; fixed nominal debt continues losing real value.
Zero inflation: prices are unchanged; fixed nominal debt keeps its real value.
Accelerating inflation: prices rise faster; fixed nominal debt gains real value.
Disinflation: prices still rise; fixed nominal debt continues losing real value.
LG-Q-3013.$correct: Disinflation: prices still rise; fixed nominal debt continues losing real value.
LG-Q-3013.feedback: A positive inflation rate still raises the price level. A slower rise is disinflation, whereas deflation is a falling price level; fixed-debt effects also depend on the relevant price comparison.
LG-Q-3013.commonError: Incorrect inference: Deflation: prices fall 5%; fixed nominal debt continues losing real value.

LG-Q-3014.q: A household owes a fixed nominal $140. Prices fall 10% while its nominal debt is unchanged. Which debt-burden comparison is correct?
options: The real burden rises exactly 10%; reciprocal percentage changes are equal
The real burden is unchanged because a fixed nominal debt is also fixed in real terms
The real burden rises about 11.1%; the same nominal repayment buys more goods
The real burden falls 10%; cheaper goods make every nominal debt smaller in real terms
LG-Q-3014.$correct: The real burden rises about 11.1%; the same nominal repayment buys more goods
LG-Q-3014.feedback: The real-debt factor is 1/.90≈1.1111. Falling prices increase, rather than decrease, the purchasing power needed to repay a fixed nominal amount.
LG-Q-3014.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The real burden rises exactly 10%; reciprocal percentage changes are equal” in this inflation tax and deflation task.

LG-Q-9121.q: Government finances $160 of purchases by creating money. Under stable velocity and fixed long-run real output, which accounting-versus-burden distinction is appropriate?
options: Government gains real resources directly; creating money leaves existing purchasing power intact.
Government gains purchasing power; inflation reduces existing money holders' real balances.
Government gains tax receipts; each money holder pays an equal statutory charge.
Government gains purchasing power; the burden is equal regardless of money holdings.
LG-Q-9121.$correct: Government gains purchasing power; inflation reduces existing money holders' real balances.
LG-Q-9121.feedback: Money financing changes claims on real goods, not productive resources themselves. Under the stated assumptions, higher prices erode real balances; exposure depends on money holdings and timing.
LG-Q-9121.commonError: Incorrect inference: Government gains real resources directly; creating money leaves existing purchasing power intact.

LG-Q-9124.q: A household holds $180 in currency while the price level rises 25%. No interest is paid. Which loss and interpretation fit the inflation-tax mechanism?
options: Real purchasing power falls 25%; the price rise is the purchasing-power loss.
Nominal cash falls 25%; inflation removes currency through an implicit tax bill.
Real purchasing power falls 20%; nominal cash is unchanged without a tax bill.
Real purchasing power is unchanged; holding the same nominal cash preserves its value.
LG-Q-9124.$correct: Real purchasing power falls 20%; nominal cash is unchanged without a tax bill.
LG-Q-9124.feedback: Real balances are M/P. With nominal currency fixed and prices multiplied by 1.25, purchasing power becomes 1/1.25=.8 of its original level, a 20% loss.
LG-Q-9124.commonError: Incorrect inference: Real purchasing power falls 25%; the price rise is the purchasing-power loss.

PM2C2-ITAX-EB-001.q: The price index is 100. Inflation falls from 8% last year to 3% this year. A fixed nominal debt remains $103. At the end of this year, what initial-price purchasing-power value does that debt represent?
options: $103; a slower inflation rate leaves prices fixed
$106.19; multiply nominal debt by the new price factor
$95; subtract the five-point decline in inflation from the debt
$100; prices rose to 103 despite disinflation
PM2C2-ITAX-EB-001.feedback: This year’s 3% inflation takes the index 100→103. Deflating the 103 debt by 1.03 gives 100. Disinflation is slower price growth, not a falling price level.
PM2C2-ITAX-EB-001.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “$103; a slower inflation rate leaves prices fixed” in this inflation tax and deflation task.

PM2C2-ITAX-EB-002.q: A household owes a fixed nominal $220. Prices fall 10% while its nominal debt is unchanged. Which debt-burden comparison is correct?
options: The real burden rises exactly 10%; reciprocal percentage changes are equal
The real burden is unchanged because a fixed nominal debt is also fixed in real terms
The real burden rises about 11.1%; the same nominal repayment buys more goods
The real burden falls 10%; cheaper goods make every nominal debt smaller in real terms
PM2C2-ITAX-EB-002.$correct: The real burden rises about 11.1%; the same nominal repayment buys more goods
PM2C2-ITAX-EB-002.feedback: The real-debt factor is 1/.90≈1.1111. Falling prices increase, rather than decrease, the purchasing power needed to repay a fixed nominal amount.
PM2C2-ITAX-EB-002.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The real burden rises exactly 10%; reciprocal percentage changes are equal” in this inflation tax and deflation task.

PM2C2-ITAX-EB-003.q: Government finances $240 of purchases by creating money. Under stable velocity and fixed long-run real output, which accounting-versus-burden distinction is appropriate?
options: Government gains real resources directly; creating money leaves existing purchasing power intact.
Government gains purchasing power; inflation reduces existing money holders' real balances.
Government gains tax receipts; each money holder pays an equal statutory charge.
Government gains purchasing power; the burden is equal regardless of money holdings.
PM2C2-ITAX-EB-003.$correct: Government gains purchasing power; inflation reduces existing money holders' real balances.
PM2C2-ITAX-EB-003.feedback: Money financing changes claims on real goods, not productive resources themselves. Under the stated assumptions, higher prices erode real balances; exposure depends on money holdings and timing.
PM2C2-ITAX-EB-003.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The inflation-tax burden is identical for people regardless of how many non-interest-bearing balances they hold” in this inflation tax and deflation task.

PM2C2-ITAX-FB-005.q: A household holds $260 in currency while the price level rises 25%. No interest is paid. Which loss and interpretation fit the inflation-tax mechanism?
options: Real purchasing power falls 25%; the price rise is the purchasing-power loss.
Nominal cash falls 25%; inflation removes currency through an implicit tax bill.
Real purchasing power falls 20%; nominal cash is unchanged without a tax bill.
Real purchasing power is unchanged; holding the same nominal cash preserves its value.
PM2C2-ITAX-FB-005.$correct: Real purchasing power falls 20%; nominal cash is unchanged without a tax bill.
PM2C2-ITAX-FB-005.feedback: Real balances are M/P. With nominal currency fixed and prices multiplied by 1.25, purchasing power becomes 1/1.25=.8 of its original level, a 20% loss.
PM2C2-ITAX-FB-005.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The nominal currency balance falls 25%; inflation removes printed dollars from the wallet” in this inflation tax and deflation task.

PM2C2-ITAX-FB-006.q: A borrower owes a fixed $1,000. Compare a 10% price-level increase with a 10% price-level decrease, from an initial index 100. Which real-debt comparison uses the correct denominators?
options: Exactly $1,000 in both; a fixed nominal contract is also fixed in real terms
About $909 after inflation and $1,111 after deflation; equal opposite price percentages have asymmetric real-debt effects
Exactly $900 and $1,100; subtract the percentage directly from the debt
About $1,111 and $909; inflation increases the real debt burden
PM2C2-ITAX-FB-006.$correct: About $909 after inflation and $1,111 after deflation; equal opposite price percentages have asymmetric real-debt effects
PM2C2-ITAX-FB-006.feedback: Real debt is 1000/1.1≈909 and 1000/.9≈1111. A fixed nominal promise changes purchasing-power value when the price level changes.
PM2C2-ITAX-FB-006.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Exactly $1,000 in both; a fixed nominal contract is also fixed in real terms” in this inflation tax and deflation task.

PM2C2-ITAX-LB-001.q: A household owes a fixed nominal $300. Prices fall 10% while its nominal debt is unchanged. Which debt-burden comparison is correct?
options: The real burden rises about 11.1%; the same nominal repayment buys more goods
The real burden falls 10%; cheaper goods make every nominal debt smaller in real terms
The real burden rises exactly 10%; reciprocal percentage changes are equal
The real burden is unchanged because a fixed nominal debt is also fixed in real terms
PM2C2-ITAX-LB-001.$correct: The real burden rises about 11.1%; the same nominal repayment buys more goods
PM2C2-ITAX-LB-001.feedback: The real-debt factor is 1/.90≈1.1111. Falling prices increase, rather than decrease, the purchasing power needed to repay a fixed nominal amount.
PM2C2-ITAX-LB-001.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The real burden falls 10%; cheaper goods make every nominal debt smaller in real terms” in this inflation tax and deflation task.

ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3000.q: An economy starts at natural unemployment. Unexpected demand expansion raises inflation and lowers unemployment; expected inflation and supply conditions initially stay fixed. Which first-stage and later-stage account is consistent?
options: First move along LRPC; later expectations rotate it down, lowering natural unemployment.
First shift SRPC down; later inflation falls further, preserving lower unemployment.
First move along SRPC; later expectations shift it up, restoring natural unemployment.
First shift SRPC up; later expectations shift LRPC left, preserving lower unemployment.
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3000.$correct: First move along SRPC; later expectations shift it up, restoring natural unemployment.
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3000.feedback: A demand shock with fixed expectations moves along a given SRPC. When higher inflation enters expectations, the curve shifts up; the initial unemployment gain need not persist.
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3000.commonError: Incorrect inference: First move along LRPC; later expectations rotate it down, lowering natural unemployment.

ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3001.q: Use inflation = expected inflation − 0.5×(unemployment−5), with rates in percent. Expected inflation is 3%. A policy moves unemployment from 5% to 3%. Which result and condition matter?
options: Inflation is 4%; this result survives fully adjusted expectations unchanged.
Inflation is 4%; this curve movement assumes fixed expectations.
Inflation is 2%; lower unemployment reduces inflation with fixed expectations.
Inflation is 3%; natural unemployment fixes inflation despite the policy.
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3001.$correct: Inflation is 4%; this curve movement assumes fixed expectations.
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3001.feedback: Substitution gives 3−.5×(3−5)=4%. That is a conditional short-run relation. A later expectations change shifts the relation and invalidates a permanent-tradeoff inference.
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3001.commonError: Incorrect inference: Inflation is 4%; this result survives fully adjusted expectations unchanged.

P52B-S2-SRPC-B2-001.q: Inflation and unemployment both rise in a country. Expected inflation or supply conditions may have changed. Which diagnosis avoids calling every observation a movement along the same SRPC?
options: A positive demand movement fits; both variables rise along the fixed downward curve.
An upward SRPC shift fits; a movement along the fixed downward curve does not.
A downward SRPC shift fits; higher unemployment establishes lower inflation expectations.
An upward-sloping LRPC fits; two observed outcomes establish the long-run relation.
P52B-S2-SRPC-B2-001.$correct: An upward SRPC shift fits; a movement along the fixed downward curve does not.
P52B-S2-SRPC-B2-001.feedback: Along a fixed downward SRPC, inflation and unemployment move in opposite directions. A shifted short-run relation can produce simultaneous increases; more evidence is needed to isolate supply from expectations.
P52B-S2-SRPC-B2-001.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The observations prove the LRPC slopes upward because every pair of data points defines the long-run relation” in this short run phillips curve task.

PM2A-SRPC-EB-007.q: Two countries each employ 160 workers and have identical natural unemployment. Both reduce demand, but one begins with higher expected inflation. Under parallel SRPCs and unchanged expectations during the adjustment, which comparison is supported?
options: At a common unemployment rate, inflation must be equal because natural unemployment is equal
The high-expectations country has lower inflation at every unemployment rate because expectations reverse the tradeoff
Reducing demand necessarily shifts both LRPCs right by the same amount
At a common unemployment rate, the high-expectations country retains higher inflation; equal unemployment does not identify one common SRPC
PM2A-SRPC-EB-007.$correct: At a common unemployment rate, the high-expectations country retains higher inflation; equal unemployment does not identify one common SRPC
PM2A-SRPC-EB-007.feedback: Expected inflation shifts the SRPC vertically. A common natural rate fixes the long-run unemployment benchmark, not the short-run inflation intercept. Compare the curves rather than treating both observations as points on one curve.
PM2A-SRPC-EB-007.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “At a common unemployment rate, inflation must be equal because natural unemployment is equal” in this short run phillips curve task.

PM2A-SRPC-EB-008.q: An expected demand expansion raises actual and expected inflation together, with no supply shock or labor-market reform. Can the initial surprise-inflation unemployment gain be inferred?
options: Yes; expected inflation shifts the long-run curve left and lowers natural unemployment.
No; expected demand expansion necessarily reduces actual inflation below its initial rate.
No; equal actual and expected inflation supplies no inflation surprise to push unemployment below natural.
Yes; any higher actual inflation implies the same unemployment gain regardless of expectations.
PM2A-SRPC-EB-008.$correct: No; equal actual and expected inflation supplies no inflation surprise to push unemployment below natural.
PM2A-SRPC-EB-008.feedback: In the expectations-augmented Phillips model, the temporary unemployment deviation depends on inflation relative to expectations. Equal increases in the two do not supply the surprise that generated the original short-run gain.
PM2A-SRPC-EB-008.commonError: Incorrect inference: Yes; any higher actual inflation implies the same unemployment gain regardless of expectations.

PM2A-SRPC-EB-009.q: Use π=πe−0.5(u−5), with rates in percent. Actual inflation is 4% and unemployment is 3%. What expectation is consistent, and does that outcome locate the economy on LRPC?
options: Expected inflation is 2%; lower unemployment must reduce inflation below expectations.
Expected inflation is 3%; unemployment below 5% places the outcome off LRPC.
Expected inflation is 5%; unemployment below 5% places the outcome on LRPC.
Expected inflation is 4%; actual inflation alone identifies expectations and the long run.
PM2A-SRPC-EB-009.$correct: Expected inflation is 3%; unemployment below 5% places the outcome off LRPC.
PM2A-SRPC-EB-009.feedback: Rearrange to πe=π+0.5(u−5)=4+0.5(3−5)=3%. The natural benchmark is 5%; observed unemployment of 3% is a short-run deviation, not a point on the vertical LRPC.
PM2A-SRPC-EB-009.commonError: Incorrect inference: Expected inflation is 5%; unemployment below 5% places the outcome on LRPC.

PM2A-SRPC-FB-010.q: Inflation and unemployment rise together. Analysts disagree between an adverse supply shock and higher inflation expectations. Do the two outcomes alone identify which mechanism caused the shift?
options: No; either can worsen the short-run relation, so additional evidence must distinguish the cause.
Yes; rising unemployment proves a pure favorable demand shock along an unchanged curve.
Yes; rising inflation proves expectations were unchanged during the observation.
No; neither mechanism can shift the short-run Phillips curve at all.
PM2A-SRPC-FB-010.$correct: No; either can worsen the short-run relation, so additional evidence must distinguish the cause.
PM2A-SRPC-FB-010.feedback: Both adverse supply conditions and higher expected inflation can shift the SRPC upward. Observing higher inflation with higher unemployment rejects a pure movement along one fixed downward curve, but does not by itself distinguish the two shift causes.
PM2A-SRPC-FB-010.commonError: Incorrect inference: Yes; rising unemployment proves a pure favorable demand shock along an unchanged curve.

PM2A-SRPC-FB-011.q: Two countries each employ 240 workers and have identical natural unemployment. Both reduce demand, but one begins with higher expected inflation. Under parallel SRPCs and unchanged expectations during the adjustment, which comparison is supported?
options: At a common unemployment rate, inflation must be equal because natural unemployment is equal
The high-expectations country has lower inflation at every unemployment rate because expectations reverse the tradeoff
Reducing demand necessarily shifts both LRPCs right by the same amount
At a common unemployment rate, the high-expectations country retains higher inflation; equal unemployment does not identify one common SRPC
PM2A-SRPC-FB-011.$correct: At a common unemployment rate, the high-expectations country retains higher inflation; equal unemployment does not identify one common SRPC
PM2A-SRPC-FB-011.feedback: Expected inflation shifts the SRPC vertically. A common natural rate fixes the long-run unemployment benchmark, not the short-run inflation intercept. Compare the curves rather than treating both observations as points on one curve.
PM2A-SRPC-FB-011.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “At a common unemployment rate, inflation must be equal because natural unemployment is equal” in this short run phillips curve task.

PM2A-SRPC-FB-012.q: After a demand surprise lowers unemployment, expectations fully catch up while productive capacity is unchanged. A report describes the return to natural unemployment as a reversal of the original demand increase. Which correction is needed?
options: Expectations adjustment permanently lowers natural unemployment below the initial benchmark.
Return to natural unemployment requires prices to fall back to their original level.
Expectations adjustment can reverse the real gain even if higher demand and inflation persist.
Return to natural unemployment proves nominal demand returned to its old level.
PM2A-SRPC-FB-012.$correct: Expectations adjustment can reverse the real gain even if higher demand and inflation persist.
PM2A-SRPC-FB-012.feedback: The upward adjustment of inflation expectations removes the initial surprise. Unemployment can return to natural at a higher sustained inflation rate without reversal of the nominal demand expansion or the price-level increase.
PM2A-SRPC-FB-012.commonError: Incorrect inference: Return to natural unemployment proves nominal demand returned to its old level.

PM2A-SRPC-LB-013.q: Use π=πe−0.5(u−5). Expectations rise from 3% to 4% after a demand surprise. If actual inflation is held at 4%, what happens to unemployment, and what inflation would retain u=3%?
options: Unemployment remains 3%; retaining 3% requires no inflation increase beyond 4%.
Unemployment rises to 7%; retaining 3% would require inflation of 3%.
Unemployment returns to 5%; retaining 3% would require inflation of 4%.
Unemployment returns to 5%; retaining 3% would require inflation of 5%.
PM2A-SRPC-LB-013.$correct: Unemployment returns to 5%; retaining 3% would require inflation of 5%.
PM2A-SRPC-LB-013.feedback: With π=πe=4%, the equation gives u=5%. To retain u=3% when πe=4%, actual inflation must be 4−0.5(3−5)=5%. Updated expectations change the inflation required for the same short-run unemployment target.
PM2A-SRPC-LB-013.commonError: Incorrect inference: Unemployment remains 3%; retaining 3% requires no inflation increase beyond 4%.

PM2A-SRPC-LB-014.q: After an adverse supply shock, policymakers hold unemployment at its former natural rate by supporting demand. Inflation rises. Does unchanged unemployment prove the short-run Phillips relation stayed fixed?
options: No; unchanged unemployment proves natural unemployment permanently fell.
Yes; demand support eliminates the supply shock rather than changing the chosen outcome.
No; policy can offset the unemployment effect while inflation reveals a worse short-run relation.
Yes; any SRPC shift must change unemployment even when policymakers adjust demand.
PM2A-SRPC-LB-014.$correct: No; policy can offset the unemployment effect while inflation reveals a worse short-run relation.
PM2A-SRPC-LB-014.feedback: An outcome reflects both the shock and the response. Supporting demand can hold unemployment at the previous benchmark while accepting higher inflation; that observation is compatible with an upward SRPC shift.
PM2A-SRPC-LB-014.commonError: Incorrect inference: Yes; any SRPC shift must change unemployment even when policymakers adjust demand.

ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3003.q: A government seeks permanently lower unemployment by repeatedly surprising workers with higher inflation. Expected inflation eventually adapts, and labor-market structure is unchanged. Which long-run assessment is justified?
options: Unemployment stays permanently lower because the downward SRPC is also the long-run policy menu
The natural rate rises one-for-one with each price-level increase by definition
The price level must return to its original value when unemployment returns to natural
Unemployment returns toward its natural rate at higher inflation; a lasting reduction needs changed real labor-market conditions
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3003.$correct: Unemployment returns toward its natural rate at higher inflation; a lasting reduction needs changed real labor-market conditions
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3003.feedback: With expectations adjusting and the natural rate unchanged, the long-run curve is vertical. Repeated monetary surprises do not establish a permanently lower unemployment benchmark.
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3003.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Unemployment stays permanently lower because the downward SRPC is also the long-run policy menu” in this long run phillips curve task.

PM2A-LRPC-EB-012.q: Matching reform reduces natural unemployment from 6% to 5% in a labor force of 120. Aggregate-demand policy separately raises sustained inflation after expectations adjust. Which graph distinction is correct?
options: Reform moves along LRPC; inflation shifts the entire curve to the left.
Reform shifts LRPC left; inflation shifts it right by reversing the reform.
Reform shifts LRPC left; inflation selects another point on that new curve.
Reform and inflation both move along the same downward-sloping long-run curve.
PM2A-LRPC-EB-012.$correct: Reform shifts LRPC left; inflation selects another point on that new curve.
PM2A-LRPC-EB-012.feedback: Structural changes in matching affect the natural rate and shift LRPC. A different sustained inflation rate with expectations adjusted does not itself determine natural unemployment.
PM2A-LRPC-EB-012.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both effects are movements along a downward-sloping LRPC” in this long run phillips curve task.

PM2A-LRPC-EB-013.q: Actual unemployment is 4% when the natural rate is 5%. Inflation expectations are temporarily below actual inflation. Which future comparison is conditional on unchanged real labor-market structure?
options: As expectations catch up, unemployment must become zero because the initial gap was negative
As expectations catch up, unemployment can return to 5%; the initial 4% does not prove LRPC shifted left
As expectations catch up, unemployment must stay 4%; observed unemployment defines the natural rate
As expectations catch up, LRPC becomes horizontal because monetary policy determines all employment
PM2A-LRPC-EB-013.$correct: As expectations catch up, unemployment can return to 5%; the initial 4% does not prove LRPC shifted left
PM2A-LRPC-EB-013.feedback: A temporary below-natural unemployment rate can be a demand/expectations gap. Without a structural change, adjustment does not require a new natural rate.
PM2A-LRPC-EB-013.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “As expectations catch up, unemployment must become zero because the initial gap was negative” in this long run phillips curve task.

PM2A-LRPC-EB-014.q: Two economies each end a disinflation at different sustained inflation rates but the same natural unemployment rate. Both have fully adjusted expectations and identical labor-market structure. Which inference is consistent?
options: The long-run benchmark is consistent; differing transition costs remain possible.
The lower-inflation economy must have a lower long-run unemployment benchmark.
The higher-inflation economy must have lower unemployment along the long-run curve.
The shared long-run benchmark requires equal cumulative transition costs in both economies.
PM2A-LRPC-EB-014.$correct: The long-run benchmark is consistent; differing transition costs remain possible.
PM2A-LRPC-EB-014.feedback: LRPC fixes the long-run unemployment benchmark under these assumptions, not inflation or the route taken. Different expectations/timing paths can produce different transition costs.
PM2A-LRPC-EB-014.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The economy with lower inflation must have lower natural unemployment” in this long run phillips curve task.

PM2A-LRPC-FB-016.q: Officials promise a constant inflation rate above the public's former expectation and permanently lower unemployment. Expectations eventually equal the promised rate. Which component of the promise fails under unchanged labor-market structure?
options: The unemployment gain strengthens; correctly anticipated inflation creates a larger surprise.
The permanent unemployment gain fails; fully anticipated inflation leaves unemployment at natural.
The constant inflation rate is impossible; natural unemployment requires zero inflation.
The natural unemployment benchmark disappears; anticipated inflation determines productive capacity.
PM2A-LRPC-FB-016.$correct: The permanent unemployment gain fails; fully anticipated inflation leaves unemployment at natural.
PM2A-LRPC-FB-016.feedback: Once expected inflation equals actual inflation, the original surprise disappears. Under unchanged labor-market structure, the long-run benchmark remains natural unemployment; positive steady inflation is compatible with it.
PM2A-LRPC-FB-016.commonError: Incorrect inference: The constant inflation rate is impossible; natural unemployment requires zero inflation.

PM2A-LRPC-FB-017.q: Matching reform reduces natural unemployment from 6% to 5% in a labor force of 200. Aggregate-demand policy separately raises sustained inflation after expectations adjust. Which graph distinction is correct?
options: Reform shifts LRPC left; inflation selects another point on that new curve.
Reform moves along LRPC; inflation shifts the entire curve to the left.
Reform shifts LRPC left; inflation shifts it right by reversing the reform.
Reform and inflation both move along the same downward-sloping long-run curve.
PM2A-LRPC-FB-017.$correct: Reform shifts LRPC left; inflation selects another point on that new curve.
PM2A-LRPC-FB-017.feedback: Structural changes in matching affect the natural rate and shift LRPC. A different sustained inflation rate with expectations adjusted does not itself determine natural unemployment.
PM2A-LRPC-FB-017.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The reform moves along a fixed LRPC; demand policy shifts LRPC left” in this long run phillips curve task.

PM2A-LRPC-LB-018.q: Unemployment is below the original natural rate during a demand boom. Later it stays low after expectations adjust, but matching institutions have improved. Which comparison prevents misattributing the persistent gain?
options: Infer permanently lower inflation; improved matching forces all nominal prices to fall.
A lower natural rate can sustain gains that surprise demand alone cannot.
Use the original natural rate forever; reforms cannot affect a long-run unemployment benchmark.
Credit demand alone; expectations adjustment preserves any original surprise unemployment gain.
PM2A-LRPC-LB-018.$correct: A lower natural rate can sustain gains that surprise demand alone cannot.
PM2A-LRPC-LB-018.feedback: If real labor-market structure changes, the natural benchmark can change. Persistence of lower unemployment then need not refute the expectations-adjusted Phillips model; the reform's effect must be separated from the temporary demand surprise.
PM2A-LRPC-LB-018.commonError: Incorrect inference: Use the original natural rate forever; reforms cannot affect a long-run unemployment benchmark.

PM2A-LRPC-LB-020.q: Two economies finish disinflation with identical inflation and natural unemployment rates. Their records show different cumulative output losses. Is that combination inconsistent with a vertical LRPC?
options: No; identical long-run endpoints can be reached through different costly transition paths.
Yes; a vertical LRPC requires identical output losses at every point in both transitions.
No; different losses prove their final natural unemployment rates were actually different.
Yes; positive output losses imply that the long-run curve slopes downward.
PM2A-LRPC-LB-020.$correct: No; identical long-run endpoints can be reached through different costly transition paths.
PM2A-LRPC-LB-020.feedback: LRPC describes the fully adjusted unemployment-inflation relation, not a unique transition path. Credibility, contracts and policy timing can produce different cumulative losses even when both economies reach the same endpoint.
PM2A-LRPC-LB-020.commonError: Incorrect inference: Yes; a vertical LRPC requires identical output losses at every point in both transitions.

PM2A-LRPC-MB-015.q: A labor-market reform lowers natural unemployment while a monetary expansion raises inflation. How could a report mistakenly credit monetary expansion for a permanent unemployment gain?
options: By distinguishing the reform's benchmark change from the monetary policy's nominal effect.
By checking whether expectations have caught up before interpreting the unemployment observation.
By comparing labor-market structure before and after the reform rather than using inflation alone.
By attributing the reform's change in the natural benchmark to the simultaneous demand expansion.
PM2A-LRPC-MB-015.$correct: By attributing the reform's change in the natural benchmark to the simultaneous demand expansion.
PM2A-LRPC-MB-015.feedback: Simultaneous events do not identify a single cause. A real matching or skill reform can lower natural unemployment; demand expansion alone does not establish that structural change. The comparison must separate the two mechanisms.
PM2A-LRPC-MB-015.commonError: Incorrect inference: By distinguishing the reform's benchmark change from the monetary policy's nominal effect.

ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3006.q: Use inflation = expected inflation − (unemployment−5) + supply offset. Unemployment is 6%, actual inflation 4%, and an independently measured temporary supply offset is +2 points. What is identified?
options: Expected inflation is 3%; without the offset measurement the data identify only expected inflation plus the offset
Expected inflation is 5%; without the offset measurement expectations are still separately identified
Expected inflation is 1%; subtract the unemployment gap and offset from actual inflation
Expected inflation is 4%; actual inflation equals expected inflation away from natural unemployment
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3006.$correct: Expected inflation is 3%; without the offset measurement the data identify only expected inflation plus the offset
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3006.feedback: 4=πe−1+2 gives πe=3. Without a measured offset, only πe+offset=5 is identified. Observed inflation and unemployment alone cannot separate these two vertical-shift mechanisms.
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3006.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Expected inflation is 5%; without the offset measurement expectations are still separately identified” in this phillips curve expectations task.

P52B-S2-PCEXP-B2-001.q: In an economy, an oil-price shock raises inflation while contracts reflect old expectations. The oil shock later ends, but expected inflation has risen and remains above its original level. What can be concluded about the final SRPC?
options: At the original curve; removing the supply shock also removes expectation persistence.
Above the original curve; comparison with the shock-period curve needs magnitudes.
Below the original curve; ending a temporary shock reverses both inflationary forces.
Above the shock-period curve; the expectations effect necessarily exceeds the removed shock.
P52B-S2-PCEXP-B2-001.$correct: Above the original curve; comparison with the shock-period curve needs magnitudes.
P52B-S2-PCEXP-B2-001.feedback: The final curve retains the expectation increase but loses the temporary supply offset. It is above the original; comparison with the shock period needs both magnitudes.
P52B-S2-PCEXP-B2-001.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “It lies below the original curve because the physical shock was temporary” in this phillips curve expectations task.

PM2A-EXP-EB-005.q: Wage contracts were written for 5% inflation. A credible announcement lowers forecasts to 2%, but those contracts cannot reset this year. Which qualification prevents overstating the announcement's immediate effect?
options: Fixed contracts can preserve current costs; lower forecasts help later adjustment.
Fixed contracts immediately reset; credible forecasts eliminate current adjustment costs.
Fixed contracts permanently fix forecasts; lower expectations cannot aid later adjustment.
Fixed contracts lower natural unemployment; credible forecasts shift the long-run curve left.
PM2A-EXP-EB-005.$correct: Fixed contracts can preserve current costs; lower forecasts help later adjustment.
PM2A-EXP-EB-005.feedback: Credibility may affect expectations, but fixed contracts delay the associated nominal adjustment. The timing assumption matters; a forecast change alone does not guarantee a costless immediate disinflation.
PM2A-EXP-EB-005.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Credibility guarantees every nominal contract instantly resets even though the stem rules it out” in this phillips curve expectations task.

PM2A-EXP-EB-006.q: Workers repeatedly observe inflation above their forecasts. Supply conditions and natural unemployment are unchanged. Which adaptation and policy implication follow?
options: Higher forecasts shift SRPC down; repeating inflation permanently lowers unemployment further
Higher forecasts move the economy along an unchanged SRPC rather than changing its intercept
Higher forecasts shift LRPC left by the same number of points as the forecast revision
Higher forecasts shift SRPC up; repeating the same actual inflation no longer produces the original surprise-driven unemployment reduction
PM2A-EXP-EB-006.$correct: Higher forecasts shift SRPC up; repeating the same actual inflation no longer produces the original surprise-driven unemployment reduction
PM2A-EXP-EB-006.feedback: Once higher inflation is expected, the short-run curve shifts upward. Maintaining an old actual inflation rate then produces less surprise, so the original temporary unemployment benefit fades.
PM2A-EXP-EB-006.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Higher forecasts shift SRPC down; repeating inflation permanently lowers unemployment further” in this phillips curve expectations task.

PM2A-EXP-EB-007.q: Use π=πe−(u−5)+s. Actual inflation is 4% at unemployment 6%. Without information about s, a student reports expected inflation as exactly 5%. Which qualification is necessary?
options: Expected inflation is exactly 4% whenever actual inflation is 4%
A positive supply offset implies a higher expectation estimate at the same inflation and unemployment
5% follows only if s=0; a positive supply offset implies a lower expectation estimate
5% is exact for every supply offset because actual inflation is given
PM2A-EXP-EB-007.$correct: 5% follows only if s=0; a positive supply offset implies a lower expectation estimate
PM2A-EXP-EB-007.feedback: Rearrange to πe=4+(6−5)−s=5−s. Ignoring an unknown supply offset treats an assumption as an observed fact.
PM2A-EXP-EB-007.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Expected inflation is exactly 4% whenever actual inflation is 4%” in this phillips curve expectations task.

PM2A-EXP-FB-009.q: An adverse oil shock ends. Expected inflation also returns fully to its original level, with natural unemployment unchanged. How does this differ from a case where expectations remain elevated?
options: SRPC stays above its original position in both cases; temporary oil shocks permanently fix the curve.
LRPC shifts left only when expectations normalize; expected inflation determines natural unemployment.
SRPC falls below its original position; removing the shock reverses it into a permanent subsidy.
SRPC returns to its original position; persistent expectations would leave it above that position.
PM2A-EXP-FB-009.$correct: SRPC returns to its original position; persistent expectations would leave it above that position.
PM2A-EXP-FB-009.feedback: Both the supply offset and expectations contributed to the short-run curve. Removing the shock and restoring original expectations removes both shifts; if expectations stay high, their upward shift remains.
PM2A-EXP-FB-009.commonError: Incorrect inference: SRPC stays above its original position in both cases; temporary oil shocks permanently fix the curve.

PM2A-EXP-LB-011.q: A credible target lowers expectations immediately, but nominal wages cannot reset for one year. Officials propose an equally immediate, large demand contraction and promise no output loss. Which sequencing change would most directly address the stated conflict?
options: Coordinate the restraint with contract adjustment; credibility alone does not instantly change locked-in nominal costs
Increase the contraction before wages reset because credibility removes every nominal rigidity
Raise expected inflation back to its old level to shift SRPC down immediately
Treat the old contracts as lower natural unemployment and use the new natural rate as the target
PM2A-EXP-LB-011.$correct: Coordinate the restraint with contract adjustment; credibility alone does not instantly change locked-in nominal costs
PM2A-EXP-LB-011.feedback: A belief change and a contract-cost change can occur at different times. The no-loss promise overlooks that timing mismatch; coordinating adjustment addresses it without assuming an altered natural rate.
PM2A-EXP-LB-011.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Increase the contraction before wages reset because credibility removes every nominal rigidity” in this phillips curve expectations task.

PM2A-EXP-LB-012.q: A government repeatedly uses surprise demand expansion to hold unemployment below natural. Wage setters begin anticipating the next expansion. Compare continuing the same actual inflation rate with generating a fresh surprise.
options: Anticipated inflation preserves the gain; expectations adjustment permanently lowers natural unemployment.
Anticipated inflation loses the gain; a fresh surprise must fall below updated expectations.
Anticipated inflation preserves the gain; a fresh surprise shifts the long-run curve left.
Anticipated inflation loses the gain; a fresh surprise must exceed updated expectations.
PM2A-EXP-LB-012.$correct: Anticipated inflation loses the gain; a fresh surprise must exceed updated expectations.
PM2A-EXP-LB-012.feedback: Once the higher rate is expected, the short-run surprise disappears. Repeating the gain requires exceeding the updated expectation; under repeated adjustment this can mean accelerating inflation rather than a stable long-run tradeoff.
PM2A-EXP-LB-012.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The same anticipated inflation permanently lowers natural unemployment; a new surprise is unnecessary” in this phillips curve expectations task.

ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3009.q: A country reduces inflation from 8% to 3% through demand restraint. Prices keep rising, and unemployment temporarily exceeds natural. Which diagnosis includes all three observations?
options: Deflation; prices fall; excess unemployment indicates temporary real costs.
Disinflation; prices still rise; excess unemployment indicates temporary real costs.
Disinflation; prices still rise; excess unemployment implies no real cost.
Disinflation; prices are unchanged; excess unemployment represents permanently lower potential.
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3009.$correct: Disinflation; prices still rise; excess unemployment indicates temporary real costs.
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3009.feedback: Disinflation lowers the inflation rate, not necessarily the price level. With sticky expectations or contracts, demand restraint can temporarily lower output and raise unemployment.
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3009.commonError: Incorrect inference: Deflation; prices fall; excess unemployment indicates temporary real costs.

P52B-S1-DIS-B3-001.q: Two plans each lower inflation four points. A rapid plan loses 8% of one year's output cumulatively; a gradual plan loses 6%. Which comparison is supported, and what is not established?
options: Ratios: gradual 0, rapid 2; spreading losses removes the gradual plan's cost.
Ratios: gradual 1.5, rapid 2; timing constraints still matter for selection.
Ratios: gradual 2, rapid 1.5; fewer calendar years establish lower cumulative cost.
Ratios: gradual 4, rapid 4; equal inflation reductions establish equal costs per point.
P52B-S1-DIS-B3-001.$correct: Ratios: gradual 1.5, rapid 2; timing constraints still matter for selection.
P52B-S1-DIS-B3-001.feedback: Using the stated cumulative-loss convention: rapid 8/4=2, gradual 6/4=1.5. Timing, uncertainty and other constraints are additional evaluation margins.
P52B-S1-DIS-B3-001.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The gradual plan is costless because spreading losses across years removes them from the sum” in this disinflation and policy task.

PM2A-DIS-EB-012.q: A credible disinflation announcement lowers expectations before demand falls; contracts can reset immediately. Compare this with identical demand restraint under fixed old expectations.
options: Earlier contract adjustment increases the initial unemployment excursion by shifting SRPC upward.
Earlier contract adjustment leaves the excursion unchanged because expectations do not affect wages.
Earlier contract adjustment permanently lowers natural unemployment despite unchanged labor-market structure.
Earlier contract adjustment can reduce the initial unemployment excursion for that restraint.
PM2A-DIS-EB-012.$correct: Earlier contract adjustment can reduce the initial unemployment excursion for that restraint.
PM2A-DIS-EB-012.feedback: Lower expectations shift SRPC down before the contraction moves the economy along it. This can reduce the short-run output/employment cost, but is conditional on the explicitly rapid contract adjustment.
PM2A-DIS-EB-012.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Earlier adjustment must raise the unemployment excursion because lower expected inflation shifts SRPC up” in this disinflation and policy task.

PM2A-DIS-EB-013.q: After disinflation, unemployment returns to its original natural rate and the inflation rate stabilizes at 2%. The price index is now 180, compared with 160 before. Which claim is supported?
options: Unemployment costs persist; the higher price level establishes continuing excess unemployment.
Unemployment costs have unwound; inflation of 2% makes the price index fall.
Unemployment costs have unwound; the price level remains higher and is still rising.
Unemployment costs cannot unwind; returning to natural requires the old price level.
PM2A-DIS-EB-013.$correct: Unemployment costs have unwound; the price level remains higher and is still rising.
PM2A-DIS-EB-013.feedback: A successful reduction in positive inflation need not undo earlier price increases. Longer-run labor adjustment and the cumulative price-level path are different outcomes.
PM2A-DIS-EB-013.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “A higher price index proves disinflation failed regardless of the lower inflation rate” in this disinflation and policy task.

PM2A-DIS-EB-014.q: Inflation falls from 8% to 3%, and later to −1%. A report calls both transitions identical disinflation outcomes for the price level. Which distinction is needed?
options: Prices rise in both periods; the sign of the inflation rate affects only unemployment.
At 3% prices still rise; at −1% they fall, so only the latter is deflation.
At 3% prices fall; at −1% they rise, so only the former is deflation.
Prices fall in both periods; any reduction in inflation establishes deflation.
PM2A-DIS-EB-014.$correct: At 3% prices still rise; at −1% they fall, so only the latter is deflation.
PM2A-DIS-EB-014.feedback: Disinflation is a reduction in inflation. A still-positive rate means a rising price level; a negative rate means a falling price level. Crossing zero therefore changes the direction of prices even though inflation fell in both transitions.
PM2A-DIS-EB-014.commonError: Incorrect inference: At 3% prices fall; at −1% they rise, so only the former is deflation.

PM2A-DIS-FB-016.q: A rapid disinflation loses 5% of annual output and cuts inflation 2 points. A gradual plan loses 6% and cuts inflation 3 points. Which plan has the lower cost per inflation point?
options: Rapid: 5 versus gradual 6; the inflation reductions are irrelevant
Both have ratio 1 because each plan reduces inflation
Gradual: 2 versus rapid 2.5, despite greater total loss
Rapid: 2.5 versus gradual 2, because a larger ratio is more efficient
PM2A-DIS-FB-016.$correct: Gradual: 2 versus rapid 2.5, despite greater total loss
PM2A-DIS-FB-016.feedback: Rapid 5/2=2.5, gradual 6/3=2. Different targets require comparison per point rather than total loss alone.
PM2A-DIS-FB-016.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Rapid: 5 versus gradual 6; the inflation reductions are irrelevant” in this disinflation and policy task.

PM2A-DIS-FB-017.q: Two countries announce identical demand restraint. In A, expectations fall promptly and wages can reset; in B, expectations remain high. What can be predicted about transition costs, without a numerical Phillips slope?
options: Both must have identical costs because the announced demand restraint is identical
A can face a smaller output cost, but an exact sacrifice-ratio difference is not identified
A must have exactly zero output cost because any credible announcement is costless
B must have the lower cost because higher expectations shift SRPC down
PM2A-DIS-FB-017.$correct: A can face a smaller output cost, but an exact sacrifice-ratio difference is not identified
PM2A-DIS-FB-017.feedback: Faster downward expectations adjustment shifts A’s short-run tradeoff favorably. Without the relevant response sizes, that directional advantage does not identify an exact cost or prove zero cost.
PM2A-DIS-FB-017.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both must have identical costs because the announced demand restraint is identical” in this disinflation and policy task.

PM2A-DIS-LB-018.q: After disinflation, unemployment returns to its original natural rate and the inflation rate stabilizes at 2%. The price index is now 260, compared with 240 before. Which claim is supported?
options: Unemployment costs persist; the higher price level establishes continuing excess unemployment.
Unemployment costs have unwound; inflation of 2% makes the price index fall.
Unemployment costs have unwound; the price level remains higher and is still rising.
Unemployment costs cannot unwind; returning to natural requires the old price level.
PM2A-DIS-LB-018.$correct: Unemployment costs have unwound; the price level remains higher and is still rising.
PM2A-DIS-LB-018.feedback: A successful reduction in positive inflation need not undo earlier price increases. Longer-run labor adjustment and the cumulative price-level path are different outcomes.
PM2A-DIS-LB-018.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “A higher price index proves disinflation failed regardless of the lower inflation rate” in this disinflation and policy task.

PM2A-DIS-LB-019.q: Two disinflation plans reach the same inflation target. One has faster expectation adjustment and less cumulative excess unemployment. Does reaching the same target imply the same real transition cost?
options: Yes; any positive final inflation rate rules out real disinflation costs.
No; the path of excess unemployment can differ even with an identical final inflation rate.
Yes; final inflation alone determines all unemployment experienced during the transition.
No; lower excess unemployment proves the final natural unemployment rate changed.
PM2A-DIS-LB-019.$correct: No; the path of excess unemployment can differ even with an identical final inflation rate.
PM2A-DIS-LB-019.feedback: An endpoint does not describe the transition path. Faster expectation adjustment can reduce excess unemployment incurred on the way to the same inflation target without requiring a different natural unemployment rate.
PM2A-DIS-LB-019.commonError: Incorrect inference: Yes; final inflation alone determines all unemployment experienced during the transition.

PM2A-DIS-MB-015.q: A plan reduces inflation from 7% to 4% at sacrifice ratio 2. Another estimate assumes the same ratio but targets 3%. How much additional cumulative output loss does the more ambitious target imply?
options: 2% of annual output
1% of annual output
6% of annual output
8% of annual output
