options: The natural-rate assumption: expected inflation alone permanently shifts LRPC left to U1
The initial demand mechanism: moving c to a requires higher unemployment rather than lower
The price adjustment: expectations shift SRPC downward, so holding U1 requires steadily lower inflation
The fixed-inflation promise: expectations shift SRPC upward, so holding U1 requires renewed inflation surprises
ECON-SP-FINALBOSS-4010.$correct: The fixed-inflation promise: expectations shift SRPC upward, so holding U1 requires renewed inflation surprises
ECON-SP-FINALBOSS-4010.feedback: Once I2 is expected, b rather than a is the natural-rate equilibrium. Repeatedly holding unemployment below U2 requires inflation above the newly adjusted expectation, not simply maintaining the original higher rate.
ECON-SP-FINALBOSS-4010.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
ECON-SP-FINALBOSS-4010.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.
ECON-SP-FINALBOSS-4010.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The natural-rate assumption: expected inflation alone permanently shifts LRPC left to U1” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.

ECON-SP-FINALBOSS-4012.q: Starting at b in the LRPC graph, policymakers reduce inflation to I1 before expectations change. Compare the first location with the eventual location if expectations adapt to I1 and the natural rate stays fixed.
options: First d, eventually a; lower expected inflation permanently lowers natural unemployment to U1
First d, eventually c; the temporary unemployment rise disappears as SRPC shifts down
First c, eventually d; expectations initially change fully and later rise again
First a, eventually b; the policy first raises inflation above expectations
ECON-SP-FINALBOSS-4012.$correct: First d, eventually c; the temporary unemployment rise disappears as SRPC shifts down
ECON-SP-FINALBOSS-4012.feedback: At the old expectation, lower inflation moves b→d on SRPC2. As expected inflation falls, SRPC shifts to SRPC1; the endpoint is c at U2.
ECON-SP-FINALBOSS-4012.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
ECON-SP-FINALBOSS-4012.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.
ECON-SP-FINALBOSS-4012.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “First d, eventually a; lower expected inflation permanently lowers natural unemployment to U1” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.

ECON-SP-FINALBOSS-4013.q: At d in the LRPC graph after disinflation, compare a credible commitment that lowers expected inflation with a loss of credibility that leaves it at the old level. Actual inflation is held at I1. Which comparison follows?
options: Credible adjustment permits movement toward c at U2; unchanged expectations leave unemployment at U3 on SRPC2
Credible adjustment moves toward a at U1; unchanged expectations also restore U2 automatically
Credible adjustment raises expected inflation and moves toward b; unchanged expectations move toward c
Both paths immediately reach c because holding actual inflation at I1 by itself shifts expectations
ECON-SP-FINALBOSS-4013.$correct: Credible adjustment permits movement toward c at U2; unchanged expectations leave unemployment at U3 on SRPC2
ECON-SP-FINALBOSS-4013.feedback: At I1, the old SRPC2 implies d/U3. Lowering expected inflation shifts the curve down, allowing c/U2 at the same actual inflation. Holding the target is not identical to having the target believed.
ECON-SP-FINALBOSS-4013.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
ECON-SP-FINALBOSS-4013.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.
ECON-SP-FINALBOSS-4013.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Credible adjustment moves toward a at U1; unchanged expectations also restore U2 automatically” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9107.q: The LRPC graph shows c→a after surprise demand expansion. Compare repeating that surprise to keep U1 with accepting b once I2 is expected. What is the dynamic tradeoff?
options: Holding U1 requires falling inflation surprises; accepting b keeps unemployment below natural
Both strategies keep U1 because the original surprise permanently shifts the LRPC
Holding U1 requires renewed surprises as forecasts rise; accepting b stabilizes inflation but restores U2
Holding U1 stabilizes inflation automatically; accepting b permanently reduces natural unemployment
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9107.$correct: Holding U1 requires renewed surprises as forecasts rise; accepting b stabilizes inflation but restores U2
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9107.feedback: a is below natural unemployment on the original expectations curve. As forecasts rise, sustaining that unemployment requires inflation above the updated forecasts. Accepting the higher-inflation natural-rate point b ends that repeated-surprise strategy.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9107.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9107.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9107.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Holding U1 requires falling inflation surprises; accepting b keeps unemployment below natural” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9108.q: The graph shows disinflation b→d. Suppose a credible announcement immediately lowers expectations, but existing wage contracts adjust only gradually. Which claim about d→c is justified?
options: b becomes the endpoint; contract lags prevent eventual inflation adjustment.
c remains the endpoint; contract lags can preserve transition costs.
U1/I1 becomes the endpoint; credibility lowers the natural unemployment rate.
d remains the endpoint; expectations have no effect on the short-run curve.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9108.$correct: c remains the endpoint; contract lags can preserve transition costs.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9108.feedback: Lower expectations support a downward SRPC shift and eventual c. Existing contracts can delay cost adjustment, leaving a temporary unemployment/output cost; neither a changed natural rate nor zero sacrifice follows from credibility alone.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9108.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves and a vertical long-run Phillips curve at unemployment rate U2, with labeled points a through d.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9108.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. A vertical LRPC stands at U2. SRPC1 is the lower/left downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/right downward-sloping curve. Point a is at U1/I2 on SRPC1, point b is at U2/I2 where SRPC2 meets the LRPC, point c is at U2/I1 where SRPC1 meets the LRPC, and point d is at U3/I1 on SRPC2. Dashed guides mark unemployment rates U1-U3 and inflation rates I1-I2.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9108.commonError: Incorrect inference: b becomes the endpoint; contract lags prevent eventual inflation adjustment.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9102.q: In the AD-AS graph, an adverse supply shock moves AS2 to AS1 from AD1-AS2. Compare keeping AD1 fixed with expanding demand to AD2 while AS1 persists. Which policy claim survives both comparisons?
options: Expansion restores both Y1 and P1 because any output recovery reverses the supply shock
Keeping AD1 fixed preserves Y1 while expansion creates Y2 at the same P2
Both policies produce Y3 because aggregate demand cannot affect output under unchanged LRAS
Expansion restores Y1 at P3 instead of Y3 at P2, but does not restore the original P1 price level
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9102.$correct: Expansion restores Y1 at P3 instead of Y3 at P2, but does not restore the original P1 price level
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9102.feedback: At unchanged demand the supply shock gives AD1-AS1, Y3/P2. Accommodation gives AD2-AS1, Y1/P3. It offsets the output loss through greater demand, paying a further price-level increase rather than undoing the supply constraint.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9102.imageAlt: AD-AS graph with LRAS at Y1, two aggregate-demand curves, two short-run aggregate-supply curves, and labeled gaps.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9102.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is real output Y and the vertical axis is the price level. LRAS is vertical at Y1. AD1 and AD2 slope downward, with AD2 to the right of AD1. AS1 and AS2 slope upward, with AS1 above/left of AS2. Dashed guides mark Y3 left of LRAS, Y1 on LRAS, Y2 right of LRAS, and price levels P1, P2, P3. AD1-AS2 is Y1/P1; AD1-AS1 is Y3/P2; AD2-AS2 is Y2/P2; AD2-AS1 is Y1/P3.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9102.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Expansion restores both Y1 and P1 because any output recovery reverses the supply shock” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9103.q: At AD2-AS2 in the graph, officials describe Y2 as permanent capacity growth. Assume no technology/resource change, fixed AD2 and rising expected prices. Which joint AD-AS/Phillips interpretation corrects them?
options: AD shifts back to AD1 and LRPC shifts left; both models predict a permanently lower price level
AS shifts right and SRPC shifts down; expected inflation increases productive capacity in both models
AS shifts left toward AS1 and output returns to Y1; on the Phillips side rising expectations erase the temporary below-natural unemployment gain
LRAS shifts to Y2 and SRPC shifts down; both models make the initial employment gain permanent
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9103.$correct: AS shifts left toward AS1 and output returns to Y1; on the Phillips side rising expectations erase the temporary below-natural unemployment gain
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9103.feedback: The graph keeps LRAS at Y1. Expected-price/wage adjustment moves AS2 toward AS1 with AD2 fixed. Correspondingly, rising expected inflation shifts SRPC up and unemployment returns to its unchanged natural rate.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9103.imageAlt: AD-AS graph with LRAS at Y1, two aggregate-demand curves, two short-run aggregate-supply curves, and labeled gaps.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9103.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is real output Y and the vertical axis is the price level. LRAS is vertical at Y1. AD1 and AD2 slope downward, with AD2 to the right of AD1. AS1 and AS2 slope upward, with AS1 above/left of AS2. Dashed guides mark Y3 left of LRAS, Y1 on LRAS, Y2 right of LRAS, and price levels P1, P2, P3. AD1-AS2 is Y1/P1; AD1-AS1 is Y3/P2; AD2-AS2 is Y2/P2; AD2-AS1 is Y1/P3.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9103.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “AD shifts back to AD1 and LRPC shifts left; both models predict a permanently lower price level” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9104.q: At AD1-AS1 in the graph, wage expectations gradually fall while AD1 stays fixed. Officials alternatively propose increasing AD to AD2 before wages adjust. Which comparison distinguishes self-correction from immediate demand support?
options: Both remain at Y3/P2 because only a technology change can close a recessionary gap
Self-correction reaches Y1/P1; immediate demand support reaches Y1/P3, so equal output recovery need not mean equal price outcomes
Self-correction reaches Y1/P3; demand support reaches Y1/P1, so demand expansion lowers the price level
Both reach Y2/P2 because recovery shifts LRAS to the right
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9104.$correct: Self-correction reaches Y1/P1; immediate demand support reaches Y1/P3, so equal output recovery need not mean equal price outcomes
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9104.feedback: Falling wage/price expectations shift AS1 toward AS2: AD1-AS2 is Y1/P1. Before that adjustment, AD2-AS1 is Y1/P3. Both close the gap under the stated alternatives, with different price levels and timing.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9104.imageAlt: AD-AS graph with LRAS at Y1, two aggregate-demand curves, two short-run aggregate-supply curves, and labeled gaps.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9104.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is real output Y and the vertical axis is the price level. LRAS is vertical at Y1. AD1 and AD2 slope downward, with AD2 to the right of AD1. AS1 and AS2 slope upward, with AS1 above/left of AS2. Dashed guides mark Y3 left of LRAS, Y1 on LRAS, Y2 right of LRAS, and price levels P1, P2, P3. AD1-AS2 is Y1/P1; AD1-AS1 is Y3/P2; AD2-AS2 is Y2/P2; AD2-AS1 is Y1/P3.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9104.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both remain at Y3/P2 because only a technology change can close a recessionary gap” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9109.q: In the SRPC graph, compare b→c on SRPC1 with c→f from SRPC1 to SRPC2. A report calls both changes consequences of weaker aggregate demand with unchanged expectations. Which correction is necessary?
options: b→c fits weaker demand; c→f raises inflation at unchanged unemployment and requires a shifted short-run relation
Both fit weaker demand because every higher point denotes higher unemployment
Only c→f fits weaker demand; b→c requires a supply shock at fixed unemployment
Neither can reflect demand because demand changes always shift SRPC rather than move along it
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9109.$correct: b→c fits weaker demand; c→f raises inflation at unchanged unemployment and requires a shifted short-run relation
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9109.feedback: b→c moves right/down along a given expectations curve. c and f share U3 but differ in inflation: that is a shift of the short-run relation, consistent with changed expectations or a supply shock, not the claimed fixed-curve demand movement.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9109.imageAlt: Phillips-curve graph with two downward-sloping short-run Phillips curves, labeled unemployment rates U1 through U4, inflation rates I1 through I4, and points a through f.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9109.graphDescription: The horizontal axis is unemployment rate and the vertical axis is inflation rate. SRPC1 is the lower downward-sloping curve and SRPC2 is the higher/rightward downward-sloping curve. On SRPC1, point a is at U1/I4, b at U2/I3, c at U3/I2, and d at U4/I1. On SRPC2, point f is at U3/I4 and point e is at U4/I3. Dashed guides connect the labeled points to unemployment rates U1-U4 and inflation rates I1-I4.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9109.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both fit weaker demand because every higher point denotes higher unemployment” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9114.q: The two-panel graph traces MS1→MS2 in an economy already below potential. Investment falls $40 billion with MPC=0.75. A timely fiscal program adds a total $100 billion to AD after induced effects. What net result and policy limit follow?
options: AD still falls $60 billion; the fiscal offset softens but does not reverse the contractionary monetary chain
AD rises $60 billion; any positive fiscal offset reverses the money-market contraction
AD rises $240 billion; multiply the already-total fiscal offset by four again
AD falls $160 billion; a fiscal offset cannot affect the same AD curve
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9114.$correct: AD still falls $60 billion; the fiscal offset softens but does not reverse the contractionary monetary chain
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9114.feedback: Monetary contraction reduces investment and AD: −40/(1−.75)=−160. Adding the total fiscal effect 100 gives−60. The diagram indicates the monetary channel, while the stated fiscal countershock determines the net result.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9114.imageAlt: Two-panel graph showing a leftward money-supply shift that raises the interest rate and a leftward aggregate-demand shift that reduces output at a fixed price level.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9114.graphDescription: Left panel: interest rate r is on the vertical axis and money M on the horizontal axis. A downward-sloping MD curve intersects MS1 at r1; MS2 is left of MS1 and intersects MD at the higher rate r2. Right panel: price level P is on the vertical axis and output Y on the horizontal axis. AD2 lies left of AD1. At price level P1, output is Y1 on AD1 and Y2 on AD2.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9114.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “AD rises $60 billion; any positive fiscal offset reverses the money-market contraction” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9115.q: In the money-market graph, compare e→d (MD1→MD2 together with MS1→MS2) with g→a (MD1→MD2 together with MS2→MS1). Why can one not infer the same rate response from higher money demand in both cases?
options: The first combines two upward pressures; the second combines two downward pressures, so demand is irrelevant
Both changes must lower rates because money demand rises
Both changes leave rates unchanged because all simultaneous shifts cancel
The first combines opposing rate pressures; the second combines two upward pressures, so supply direction matters
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9115.$correct: The first combines opposing rate pressures; the second combines two upward pressures, so supply direction matters
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9115.feedback: e→d raises both money demand and money supply: their separate rate effects oppose, with this drawing showing r2→r3. g→a raises demand while reducing supply, reinforcing the rate increase r1→r4. The graph-specific net result of opposing shifts is not a universal sign rule.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9115.imageAlt: Money-market graph with two vertical money-supply curves, two downward-sloping money-demand curves, and labeled interest-rate and money-quantity points.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9115.graphDescription: The vertical axis is interest rate r and the horizontal axis is quantity of money Qm. MS1 is vertical at Qm1 and MS2 is vertical to its right at Qm2. MD1 slopes downward through e at Qm1, r2 and g at Qm2, r1. MD2 is shifted right and upward and slopes downward through a at Qm1, r4 and d at Qm2, r3. Additional labeled points are b at Qm2, r4; c at Qm1, r3; and f at Qm1, r1.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARYBOSS-9115.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The first combines two upward pressures; the second combines two downward pressures, so demand is irrelevant” in this integrated macroeconomic analysis task.

ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3004.q: The LRPC graph marks U2 as natural unemployment. A demand boom moves c→a, while a separate reform would reduce structural unemployment. Which change could move the long-run benchmark itself?
options: Both must move LRPC right because lower unemployment requires higher inflation
Neither can move LRPC because the natural rate is fixed by the price level
The reform could move LRPC left; c→a alone changes actual unemployment relative to the fixed benchmark
The demand boom moves LRPC left; the reform only changes inflation along it
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3004.$correct: The reform could move LRPC left; c→a alone changes actual unemployment relative to the fixed benchmark
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3004.feedback: Demand surprises move actual unemployment around natural unemployment. A persistent change in structural unemployment can change the natural rate and hence the position of LRPC.
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3004.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both must move LRPC right because lower unemployment requires higher inflation” in this long run phillips curve task.

ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3007.q: In the LRPC graph c→a follows a demand surprise. If actual inflation stays at I2, compare full expectation adjustment with no expectation adjustment.
options: Full adjustment leads toward c/U2; unchanged expectations move it to d/U3
Full adjustment leaves it at a/U1; unchanged expectations shift LRPC left
Both lead to b immediately because actual inflation alone determines expected inflation
Full adjustment leads toward b/U2; unchanged expectations keep the economy on SRPC1 at a/U1
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3007.$correct: Full adjustment leads toward b/U2; unchanged expectations keep the economy on SRPC1 at a/U1
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3007.feedback: At I2, a is on the original SRPC1 and b is on the higher-expectation SRPC2. The unemployment endpoint depends on expectation adjustment, not solely the maintained actual rate.
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3007.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Full adjustment leads toward c/U2; unchanged expectations move it to d/U3” in this phillips curve expectations task.

ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3010.q: Starting at b, a disinflation moves to d in the LRPC graph. A forecast instead predicts c immediately. What extra assumption could justify that forecast?
options: Actual inflation falls while expected inflation rises by the same amount
Expectations and relevant wages adjust promptly to lower inflation, shifting SRPC down
Expected inflation remains fixed at its old level throughout the contraction
Natural unemployment rises to U3 when aggregate demand falls
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3010.$correct: Expectations and relevant wages adjust promptly to lower inflation, shifting SRPC down
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3010.feedback: d is the short-run result with old expectations. Immediate c would require the lower short-run curve to apply immediately, an additional adjustment assumption rather than a result of demand contraction alone.
ECON-SP-MEDIUMBOSS-3010.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Actual inflation falls while expected inflation rises by the same amount” in this disinflation and policy task.

LG-Q-9138.q: The two-panel graph shows a rate change and an investment-led AD change following a money-supply shift. Now suppose rates still respond but firms no longer change investment. Which stage fails, and does the original graph demonstrate a liquidity trap?
options: The AD-to-price link fails; the original graph proves all prices remain fixed
The rate-to-investment link fails; the original responsive money-demand graph does not demonstrate a liquidity trap
The supply-to-rate link fails; the original graph already shows a flat zero-rate money-demand segment
The reserve-accounting identity fails; the original graph proves deposits cannot change
LG-Q-9138.$correct: The rate-to-investment link fails; the original responsive money-demand graph does not demonstrate a liquidity trap
LG-Q-9138.feedback: Separate supply→interest from interest→investment. The counterfactual leaves the first working but removes the second. The original graph has responsive interest rates and is not the flat near-zero-rate case usually used to illustrate a liquidity trap.
LG-Q-9138.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The AD-to-price link fails; the original graph proves all prices remain fixed” in this monetary policy transmission task.

LG-Q-9142.q: Use the multiplier graph to distinguish the first AD shift from the induced shift. A $60 billion tax cut has MPC=.75; an alternative purchases increase is $45 billion. With the same multiplier and no crowding out, which comparison is correct?
options: Both first-round impulses are $60 billion and total shifts $240 billion, because taxes and purchases are identical
The tax cut adds only $45 billion in total, while purchases receive induced spending
Both first-round impulses are $45 billion and total shifts $180 billion, although the budget costs differ
The tax cut first adds $60 billion and ultimately $240 billion, while purchases add only $180 billion
LG-Q-9142.$correct: Both first-round impulses are $45 billion and total shifts $180 billion, although the budget costs differ
LG-Q-9142.feedback: Tax-induced first-round consumption=.75×60=45; direct purchases also add 45. The spending multiplier is 4, so both total 180. Equal demand impulses do not mean equal changes in the government budget.
LG-Q-9142.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both first-round impulses are $60 billion and total shifts $240 billion, because taxes and purchases are identical” in this fiscal policy and aggregate demand task.

PM2B3-PROD-EB-002.q: In GROWTH-01, A has output per worker about 28.53 and B about 36.37. If employment is identical, a report says doubling capital per worker from 20 to 40 doubles total output. Which correction uses both the graph and the fixed-employment condition?
options: Output rises 100%; doubling capital always doubles output even on a flattening curve
Output rises about 7.84%; subtracting productivity levels directly gives a percentage
Output falls about 21.6%; use the higher productivity as the initial value
Output rises about 27.5%, not 100%; fixed employment makes total output grow by that same percentage
PM2B3-PROD-EB-002.$correct: Output rises about 27.5%, not 100%; fixed employment makes total output grow by that same percentage
PM2B3-PROD-EB-002.feedback: With identical employment, total-output growth equals output-per-worker growth: (36.37/28.53−1)×100≈27.5%. The flattening curve does not support proportional doubling.
PM2B3-PROD-EB-002.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Output rises 100%; doubling capital always doubles output even on a flattening curve” in this productivity measurement task.

PM2B3-PROD-LB-002.q: The GROWTH-01 curve shows productivity rising from A to B. Employment could rise or fall during that move. Which part of a claim that both productivity and total output must rise is established by the graph alone?
options: Productivity rises; total output depends on the accompanying employment change.
Productivity and total output rise; higher output per worker fixes both directions.
Only total output rises; the vertical axis measures aggregate rather than per-worker output.
Neither rises; diminishing returns make additional capital reduce output per worker.
PM2B3-PROD-LB-002.$correct: Productivity rises; total output depends on the accompanying employment change.
PM2B3-PROD-LB-002.feedback: Output per worker rises from 28.53 to 36.37, but total output is productivity×workers. A workforce ratio below 28.53/36.37≈.7844 would more than offset that gain. Diminishing positive returns do not mean falling productivity.
PM2B3-PROD-LB-002.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both must rise; an increase in output per worker rules out falling total output” in this productivity measurement task.

PM2B3-SRC-EB-002.q: GROWTH-01 is steeper near A than B. Compare an equal small addition to capital per worker at each point, holding technology and other inputs per worker fixed. Which forecast is supported?
options: A larger productivity gain near A, but positive gains at both points
Equal productivity gains at both points because capital additions are equal
A larger gain near B because its initial productivity is higher
A gain near A and a loss near B because diminishing returns turn output negative
PM2B3-SRC-EB-002.$correct: A larger productivity gain near A, but positive gains at both points
PM2B3-SRC-EB-002.feedback: The slope measures the marginal productivity effect of capital deepening. The curve is positive but flatter near B: the marginal gain is smaller, not negative.
PM2B3-SRC-EB-002.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Equal productivity gains at both points because capital additions are equal” in this sources of productivity task.

PM2B3-SRC-FB-004.q: In GROWTH-01, capital deepening takes the economy A→B on one curve. A later observation lies above that curve at the same capital per worker as B. Which explanation distinguishes the two changes?
options: Both show falling marginal productivity means falling total productivity
A→B is capital deepening; the later gain requires another productive factor or technology to improve
Both are movements along the same curve caused only by more capital per worker
A→B is a technology shift; the later gain is diminishing returns to unchanged capital
PM2B3-SRC-FB-004.$correct: A→B is capital deepening; the later gain requires another productive factor or technology to improve
PM2B3-SRC-FB-004.feedback: Moving along the curve changes capital with the other determinants held fixed. Higher output at the same capital requires a changed productive condition, such as technology or human capital.
PM2B3-SRC-FB-004.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both show falling marginal productivity means falling total productivity” in this sources of productivity task.

PM2B3-POL-FB-006.q: The graph suggests high marginal returns near A, but a country at A has unreliable contract enforcement that deters investment. Compare subsidizing machines alone with improving enforcement plus investment. Which inference respects the difference between potential and realized catch-up?
options: Enforcement plus investment addresses the constraint; potential returns alone do not ensure investment.
Machine subsidies alone ensure catch-up; investors' ability to retain returns is irrelevant.
Enforcement alone reaches B immediately; additional capital and production changes are unnecessary.
Neither policy can help at A; diminishing returns eliminate the incentive to invest.
PM2B3-POL-FB-006.$correct: Enforcement plus investment addresses the constraint; potential returns alone do not ensure investment.
PM2B3-POL-FB-006.feedback: The curve describes productive potential under maintained conditions. Weak enforcement can stop capital accumulation despite high physical returns. Addressing incentives complements capital deepening; it does not mechanically manufacture the required capital.
PM2B3-POL-FB-006.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Machine subsidies alone guarantee catch-up regardless of whether investors can retain returns” in this economic growth policy task.

PM2B3-POL-LB-001.q: GROWTH-01 suggests catch-up through A→B. A planner proposes ever larger capital investment to maintain the initial growth rate indefinitely, with technology and all other productivity determinants fixed. Which alternative distinguishes a higher level from sustained growth?
options: Capital deepening preserves the initial marginal return indefinitely; research would only change nominal output
Diminishing returns imply no gain from A→B, so reducing capital is the growth strategy
Reaching B guarantees permanent growth even if all productive inputs and technology then stop changing
Capital deepening raises the level with diminishing gains; sustained productivity growth requires continuing improvements beyond capital alone
PM2B3-POL-LB-001.$correct: Capital deepening raises the level with diminishing gains; sustained productivity growth requires continuing improvements beyond capital alone
PM2B3-POL-LB-001.feedback: Diminishing returns make successive capital additions less productive. A finite catch-up level gain is not a permanent growth mechanism. Continuing technology/human-capital improvements can change the productive relation instead of relying only on movement along it.
PM2B3-POL-LB-001.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Capital deepening preserves the initial marginal return indefinitely; research would only change nominal output” in this economic growth policy task.

PM2C3-LPMM-LB-001.q: With MD2 and MS2, point b is above equilibrium d. Compare the initial asset-market adjustment with a counterfactual central-bank sale that reduces supply to MS1 before rates adjust. Which two conclusions follow?
options: Initially excess money prompts bond sales and higher rates; the sale makes g the new equilibrium at a lower rate
Initially a money shortage prompts bond sales and higher rates; the sale makes e the new equilibrium on MD1
Initially a money shortage prompts bond purchases and lower rates; the sale leaves d unchanged
Initially excess money prompts bond purchases and lower rates; the sale makes a the new equilibrium at the original higher rate
PM2C3-LPMM-LB-001.$correct: Initially excess money prompts bond purchases and lower rates; the sale makes a the new equilibrium at the original higher rate
PM2C3-LPMM-LB-001.feedback: At b under MS2/MD2, money supplied exceeds desired balances, inducing bond purchases and downward rate pressure toward d. Reducing supply to MS1 changes the relevant equilibrium to a on MD2 at r4. The policy changes the equilibrium, rather than reversing the asset adjustment at the original curves.
PM2C3-LPMM-LB-001.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Initially excess money prompts bond sales and higher rates; the sale makes g the new equilibrium at a lower rate” in this liquidity preference and money market task.

PM2D1-LRADJ-EB-002.q: At AD1-AS1 the graph places output at Y3 below potential Y1. Demand stays fixed. Which wage adjustment and output movement would close this gap?
options: Rising expected wages/costs shift AS2 toward AS1 and raise output toward Y1
Falling expected wages/costs shift AD1 toward AD2 and lower output toward Y3
Rising expected wages/costs shift LRAS toward Y3 and increase productive capacity
Falling expected wages/costs shift AS1 toward AS2 and raise output toward Y1
PM2D1-LRADJ-EB-002.$correct: Falling expected wages/costs shift AS1 toward AS2 and raise output toward Y1
PM2D1-LRADJ-EB-002.feedback: A recessionary gap puts downward pressure on expected wages/costs. With demand fixed, supply shifts right toward AS2, returning output toward Y1.
PM2D1-LRADJ-EB-002.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Rising expected wages/costs shift AS2 toward AS1 and raise output toward Y1” in this ad as equilibrium and output gaps task.

PM2D1-LRADJ-MB-004.q: At AD1-AS1/Y3, nominal wages are fixed by contracts for one year. Officials predict immediate self-correction to Y1 solely through lower wages. Which part of that prediction conflicts with the stated constraint?
options: Neither is appropriate because returning to Y1 requires LRAS to move left
The direction is appropriate but the claimed timing is not: wage-based AS adjustment must wait for contracts
The timing is appropriate but the direction is not: lower wages shift AS left
Both are appropriate because contracts cannot affect short-run supply adjustment
PM2D1-LRADJ-MB-004.$correct: The direction is appropriate but the claimed timing is not: wage-based AS adjustment must wait for contracts
PM2D1-LRADJ-MB-004.feedback: Lower wages would shift AS1 toward AS2, but fixed contracts prevent that wage mechanism from completing immediately. Distinguish eventual direction from adjustment speed.
PM2D1-LRADJ-MB-004.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Neither is appropriate because returning to Y1 requires LRAS to move left” in this long run macroeconomic self adjustment task.

PM2D1-LRADJ-FB-006.q: Demand has moved AD1→AD2 while supply remains AS2. Compare fixed AD2 with a policy that reverses demand to AD1 before expected wages rise. Which final price/output pairs follow?
options: Fixed AD2: P1/Y1; quick reversal: P3/Y1.
Fixed AD2: P2/Y2; quick reversal: P2/Y2.
Fixed AD2: P3/Y1; quick reversal: P1/Y1.
Fixed AD2: P2/Y3; quick reversal: P2/Y3.
PM2D1-LRADJ-FB-006.$correct: Fixed AD2: P3/Y1; quick reversal: P1/Y1.
PM2D1-LRADJ-FB-006.feedback: The first path moves AS2→AS1 with AD2 fixed. The second returns to AD1-AS2 before the supply response. Both recover potential, but at different price levels.
PM2D1-LRADJ-FB-006.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both give P2/Y2 because demand permanently raises potential” in this long run macroeconomic self adjustment task.

PM2D1-LRADJ-LB-002.q: At AD1-AS1/Y3, wages start falling. Before adjustment ends, demand falls further left of AD1. Which conclusion can still be drawn without the sizes of the two shifts?
options: Wages support recovery; further demand loss makes the final output change uncertain.
Wages ensure recovery to Y1; the supply shift dominates the added demand loss.
Demand ensures a further output fall; the demand shift dominates falling wages.
Both changes lower potential output; combined AD and SRAS shifts move LRAS left.
PM2D1-LRADJ-LB-002.$correct: Wages support recovery; further demand loss makes the final output change uncertain.
PM2D1-LRADJ-LB-002.feedback: Rightward AS adjustment raises output relative to unchanged demand, while a new demand contraction lowers it. Relative magnitudes determine the net output path; LRAS need not move.
PM2D1-LRADJ-LB-002.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Output must reach Y1 immediately because any rightward supply shift dominates demand” in this long run macroeconomic self adjustment task.

PMOE-FX-B3-003.q: In FX-03, supply expands and the foreign-units-per-domestic-unit rate falls from 1 to 0.8 while quantity rises 100→150. An importer faces an unchanged foreign price. Which rate, quantity and home-currency import-cost comparison is correct?
options: Domestic currency appreciates 25%, quantity rises 50%, and the home import cost falls 20%
Domestic currency depreciates 20%, quantity rises 33.3%, and the home import cost falls 25%
Domestic currency depreciates 20%, traded quantity rises 50%, and the home cost of the import rises 25%
Domestic currency depreciates 20%, quantity rises 50%, and the home import cost rises 20%
PMOE-FX-B3-003.$correct: Domestic currency depreciates 20%, traded quantity rises 50%, and the home cost of the import rises 25%
PMOE-FX-B3-003.feedback: Rate change=.8/1−1=−20%; quantity change=150/100−1=50%. Home currency per foreign unit rises from 1 to 1/.8=1.25, increasing a fixed foreign-price import cost 25%. Reciprocal percentage changes are not symmetric.
PMOE-FX-B3-003.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Domestic currency appreciates 25%, quantity rises 50%, and the home import cost falls 20%” in this foreign exchange market task.

LG-Q-9053.q: The graph shows MS1→MS2, followed by AD falling $240 billion. MPC=.75 and only investment changes autonomously. Which reverse inference identifies the investment change and its place in the chain?
options: Investment fell $960 billion after rates rose; divide the total loss by MPC
Investment fell $60 billion after rates rose; the multiplier converts that impulse to the total AD loss
Investment fell $240 billion before rates changed; the AD loss is the autonomous impulse
Investment rose $60 billion after rates fell; the money shift is expansionary
LG-Q-9053.$correct: Investment fell $60 billion after rates rose; the multiplier converts that impulse to the total AD loss
LG-Q-9053.feedback: The multiplier is 4, so the autonomous investment reduction is 240/4=60. In the graph a supply contraction raises rates, reducing investment before the induced spending response.

LG-Q-9055.q: Read the graph in reverse: policy moves MS2→MS1, lowering rates and raising investment $40 billion. A separate confidence loss reduces investment $25 billion. MPC=.5. Which net AD change follows?
options: Right $80 billion: ignore the confidence loss because rates fell
Left $30 billion: reverse the effect of a net investment increase
Right $15 billion: include both impulses but omit induced spending
Right $30 billion: multiply the net $15 billion autonomous investment rise
LG-Q-9055.$correct: Right $30 billion: multiply the net $15 billion autonomous investment rise
LG-Q-9055.feedback: Reversing the displayed contraction gives expansion. Net autonomous investment changes 40−25=15; with multiplier 2, AD rises 30. The rate response alone does not determine the size after a confidence countershock.

LG-Q-9056.q: The graph shows the same rate rise in two economies. Investment falls $20 billion in A and $5 billion in B; both have MPC=.8 and no other shocks. Which inference compares transmission strength rather than reserve accounting?
options: AD falls $25 billion in A and $100 billion in B; weaker investment sensitivity magnifies the effect
AD falls $100 billion in both; identical rate changes guarantee identical spending changes
AD falls $100 billion in A and $25 billion in B; B has weaker investment sensitivity to the rate change
AD falls $20 billion in A and $5 billion in B; the multiplier is irrelevant to rate-induced spending
LG-Q-9056.$correct: AD falls $100 billion in A and $25 billion in B; B has weaker investment sensitivity to the rate change
LG-Q-9056.feedback: The multiplier is 5, giving losses 100 and 25. The divergence arises at interest→investment, even though the preceding observed rate change and subsequent multiplier are identical.

LG-Q-9059.q: MS1→MS2 in the graph reduces investment $40 billion with MPC=.8. An immediate fiscal program adds $200 billion to AD in total after induced effects. If that fiscal program instead arrives after the monetary contraction has ended, which comparison is justified?
options: Both timings offset exactly because equal dollar effects guarantee equal stabilization
Immediate AD rises $800 billion because the total fiscal effect must be multiplied again
Immediate AD falls $200 billion because fiscal and monetary shifts cannot offset
Immediate effects offset; the delayed program can create excess demand after the original gap closes
LG-Q-9059.$correct: Immediate effects offset; the delayed program can create excess demand after the original gap closes
LG-Q-9059.feedback: The investment effect is−40/.2=−200 and the immediate total fiscal effect+200 offsets it. Equal magnitudes do not ensure stabilization if the countershock arrives at a different point in the cycle.

LG-Q-9072.q: The graph holds money demand fixed while MS1→MS2 raises rates. Now suppose money demand also falls. Without relative shift sizes, which part of the displayed rate→investment→AD prediction is still certain?
options: Supply contraction alone raises rates; the combined transmission direction remains uncertain.
Supply contraction dominates; rates rise, investment falls and aggregate demand falls.
Demand contraction dominates; rates fall, investment rises and aggregate demand rises.
The contractions cancel; rates, investment and aggregate demand all remain unchanged.
LG-Q-9072.$correct: Supply contraction alone raises rates; the combined transmission direction remains uncertain.
LG-Q-9072.feedback: Less supply raises the equilibrium rate holding demand fixed; lower demand reduces it holding supply fixed. Without magnitudes the combined rate direction, and hence the interest-sensitive spending chain, cannot be signed.

43139.q: A report defines its ratio as debt held by the public divided by annual GDP. GDP is $30 trillion and that debt is $30.3 trillion; gross federal debt is $36 trillion. Which ratio belongs in this report?
options: 101%, using debt held by the public
120%, using gross federal debt
99%, dividing GDP by public debt
20%, using the difference between the debt measures
43139.$correct: 101%, using debt held by the public
43139.feedback: 30.3/30×100=101%. The named numerator excludes the extra intragovernmental holdings included in gross debt.
43139.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “20%, using the difference between the debt measures” in this debt measures burden and fiscal data task.

43160.q: A larger deficit reduces public saving while private saving is unchanged. In a closed-economy loanable-funds model with unchanged investment demand, what pressure does this place on interest and private investment?
options: Interest rises and private investment rises
Interest falls and private investment falls
Interest rises and private investment falls
Interest falls and private investment rises
43160.$correct: Interest rises and private investment falls
43160.feedback: Lower national saving shifts loanable-funds supply left. The higher equilibrium interest rate reduces investment demanded.
43160.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Interest rises and private investment rises” in this deficits debt and government borrowing task.

43234.q: Households save more at each interest rate. In the loanable-funds market, with investment demand unchanged, which equilibrium change follows?
options: Supply shifts right, lowering interest and raising investment
Demand shifts right, raising interest and investment
Supply shifts left, raising interest and lowering investment
Demand shifts left, lowering interest and investment
43234.$correct: Supply shifts right, lowering interest and raising investment
43234.feedback: Saving supplies loanable funds. A rightward supply shift lowers their price (interest) and raises the equilibrium quantity invested.
43234.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Demand shifts right, raising interest and investment” in this loanable funds equilibrium task.

ECON-NL-CATCH-UP-EFFECT-6024.q: Two countries share technology and worker skills, but A has much less capital per worker. Both add the same small amount of capital per worker. With diminishing marginal returns, which comparison follows?
options: B gains more because its starting output is higher
Both gain the same because additions are equal
A loses output because it began with less capital
A gains more output per worker from that addition
ECON-NL-CATCH-UP-EFFECT-6024.$correct: A gains more output per worker from that addition
ECON-NL-CATCH-UP-EFFECT-6024.feedback: Under comparable other conditions, capital is more productive at the margin where it is scarcer. This is conditional catch-up potential.
ECON-NL-CATCH-UP-EFFECT-6024.commonError: Confuses a higher starting level with a higher marginal return.

ECON-NL-DIMINISHING-RETURNS-6023.q: With labor and technology fixed, successive identical machines raise output by 12, 9 and 6 units. A plan assumes a fourth adds 12. Which revision fits diminishing marginal returns?
options: Expect a gain smaller than 6 if the pattern continues
Expect a gain of 12 because the machines are identical
Expect total output to fall by 6
Expect every previous machine’s output to disappear
ECON-NL-DIMINISHING-RETURNS-6023.$correct: Expect a gain smaller than 6 if the pattern continues
ECON-NL-DIMINISHING-RETURNS-6023.feedback: Diminishing marginal returns concern successively smaller additions to output, not a fall in total output or identical gains from identical inputs.
ECON-NL-DIMINISHING-RETURNS-6023.commonError: Confuses identical physical inputs with equal marginal products.

ECON-NL-HUMAN-CAPITAL-6020.q: A factory buys machines but cannot operate them because workers lack the necessary training. Which complementary change would make the physical-capital investment usable?
options: Count the machines as natural resources
Raise product prices without changing production
Train workers to operate the new machines
Replace worker training with more idle machines
ECON-NL-HUMAN-CAPITAL-6020.$correct: Train workers to operate the new machines
ECON-NL-HUMAN-CAPITAL-6020.feedback: Training supplies complementary human capital, allowing the new physical capital to contribute to output.
ECON-NL-HUMAN-CAPITAL-6020.commonError: Treats physical capital as productive without complementary worker skills.

ECON-NL-NATURAL-RESOURCES-6021.q: A mineral deposit is discovered, but output cannot rise until transport links reach it. Which conclusion applies the natural-resource distinction?
options: Only human capital changed because discovery involves knowledge
The deposit is produced capital because it has economic value
Resource availability improved, but complementary infrastructure is needed to use it
Current productivity must already have risen by the full value of the deposit
ECON-NL-NATURAL-RESOURCES-6021.$correct: Resource availability improved, but complementary infrastructure is needed to use it
ECON-NL-NATURAL-RESOURCES-6021.feedback: The natural resource exists, but access requires produced infrastructure. A resource discovery is not itself measured production or guaranteed immediate productivity.
ECON-NL-NATURAL-RESOURCES-6021.commonError: Equates resource discovery with immediate usable output.

ECON-NL-TECHNOLOGICAL-KNOWLEDGE-6022.q: A new production method raises output with the same workforce and machines. If the method is shared with a comparable second plant, what change could occur without more physical capital?
options: Only its number of machines could rise
Its output per worker must fall
Only its nominal selling price could change
Its output per worker could rise
ECON-NL-TECHNOLOGICAL-KNOWLEDGE-6022.$correct: Its output per worker could rise
ECON-NL-TECHNOLOGICAL-KNOWLEDGE-6022.feedback: Using a better method can raise productivity at unchanged inputs; technology is distinct from adding machines.
ECON-NL-TECHNOLOGICAL-KNOWLEDGE-6022.commonError: Attributes every productivity gain to more physical capital.

ECON-NL-GROWTH-POLICY-6025.q: A country has available technology and willing investors, but contracts are rarely enforced. Which policy directly addresses this stated obstacle to productive investment?
options: Reclassify transfers as investment in the accounts
Improve reliable contract enforcement
Raise aggregate demand without changing enforcement
Restrict worker training while subsidizing consumption
ECON-NL-GROWTH-POLICY-6025.feedback: Reliable enforcement lets investors expect to retain contractual returns. This addresses the specified incentive constraint rather than merely adding short-run spending.
ECON-NL-GROWTH-POLICY-6025.commonError: Applies demand stimulus to an institutional investment constraint.

ECON-NL-PRODUCTIVITY-CALCULATION-6018.q: A team must produce 2,400 units. Productivity improves from 8 to 10 units per hour. How many labor hours are now needed?
options: 192 hours
240 hours
300 hours
24,000 hours
ECON-NL-PRODUCTIVITY-CALCULATION-6018.commonError: Multiplies output by productivity instead of dividing.

ECON-NL-REAL-GDP-PER-PERSON-6017.q: Real GDP is $3 trillion and population 100 million. If population rises to 120 million with real GDP unchanged, what is new real GDP per person?
ECON-NL-REAL-GDP-PER-PERSON-6017.feedback: Divide 3 trillion by 120 million to get 25,000. More people share unchanged real output.
ECON-NL-REAL-GDP-PER-PERSON-6017.commonError: Holds per-person GDP fixed when population changes.

ECON-NL-RULE-OF-70-6016.q: Using the Rule of 70, compare a 2% annual growth rate with 4%. What happens to approximate doubling time?
options: It rises from 17.5 to 35 years
It falls from 70 to 35 years
It stays 35 years because both rates are positive
It falls from 35 to 17.5 years
ECON-NL-RULE-OF-70-6016.feedback: 70/2=35; 70/4=17.5. Doubling the growth rate halves approximate doubling time.
ECON-NL-RULE-OF-70-6016.commonError: Makes doubling time proportional to the growth rate.

ECON-NL-INCOME-EXPENDITURE-IDENTITY-6000.q: Final domestic output sells for $210. Production income records show wages $140 and rent/interest $30. With no taxes, depreciation or discrepancy, what profit completes the income ledger?
ECON-NL-INCOME-EXPENDITURE-IDENTITY-6000.feedback: All income from producing the output sums to 210. The missing profit is 210−140−30=40.
ECON-NL-INCOME-EXPENDITURE-IDENTITY-6000.commonError: Adds spending to income instead of reconciling the two ledgers.

ECON-NL-INTERMEDIATE-VS-FINAL-GOODS-6002.q: A mill sells flour for $50 and a bakery sells the bread made from it to households for $120. The bakery’s value added is $70. Which GDP total agrees under both final-sales and value-added accounting?
ECON-NL-INTERMEDIATE-VS-FINAL-GOODS-6002.feedback: Final bread sales 120 equal mill value added 50 plus bakery value added 70. Counting flour again with final sales double-counts it.
ECON-NL-INTERMEDIATE-VS-FINAL-GOODS-6002.commonError: Counts intermediate sales again alongside final goods.

ECON-NL-GDP-COMPONENTS-IDENTITY-6003.q: A household buys a newly produced domestic car for $30,000; a firm buys a newly produced domestic machine for $20,000. Which pair enters the expenditure accounts?
ECON-NL-GDP-COMPONENTS-IDENTITY-6003.feedback: Household final purchases enter consumption; productive equipment purchased by a firm enters investment.
ECON-NL-GDP-COMPONENTS-IDENTITY-6003.commonError: Classifies durable household consumption as business investment.

ECON-NL-INVENTORY-INVESTMENT-6005.q: A factory makes $100 of new domestic output and sells $80 this period. The unsold $20 stays in inventory. What current production total is recorded?
options: $80: only sold goods count
$120: production 100 plus inventory 20
$20: only inventory is new production
$100: sales 80 plus inventory investment 20
ECON-NL-INVENTORY-INVESTMENT-6005.feedback: Unsold current production is inventory investment. Final sales 80 plus inventory accumulation 20 record the same 100 produced.
ECON-NL-INVENTORY-INVESTMENT-6005.commonError: Excludes unsold current production or counts it twice.

ECON-NL-GDP-DEFLATOR-6007.q: Nominal GDP is $180 and the GDP deflator is 120 (base 100). What real GDP value makes the output comparison use base-year prices?
ECON-NL-GDP-DEFLATOR-6007.commonError: Multiplies nominal GDP by the price index instead of deflating.

ECON-NL-NOMINAL-VS-REAL-GDP-6006.q: Real GDP per person rises, while pollution rises and leisure falls. Does the GDP gain alone establish that overall well-being improved?
options: Yes; per-person GDP measures the distribution and value of all nonmarket activity
No; those omitted dimensions could offset the measured output gain
Yes; real GDP directly includes pollution damage and leisure
No; real GDP must fall whenever leisure falls
ECON-NL-NOMINAL-VS-REAL-GDP-6006.$correct: No; those omitted dimensions could offset the measured output gain
ECON-NL-NOMINAL-VS-REAL-GDP-6006.feedback: The measured output gain is real, but GDP does not settle the valuation of lost leisure and environmental quality.
ECON-NL-NOMINAL-VS-REAL-GDP-6006.commonError: Treats real GDP per person as a complete welfare measure.

ECON-NL-CPI-CALCULATION-6009.q: A fixed basket costs $400 in the base year. If today’s CPI is 125 (base 100), what is today’s basket cost?

ECON-NL-INFLATION-RATE-6010.q: CPI rises from 125 to 150. A rent of $1,000 is adjusted by that inflation rate. What is the new rent?
ECON-NL-INFLATION-RATE-6010.commonError: Treats the index-point change as the percentage inflation rate.

ECON-NL-INFLATION-ADJUSTMENT-6014.q: A salary was $40,000 at CPI100. At CPI160 it is $60,000. How much additional salary would preserve the original purchasing power?
ECON-NL-INFLATION-ADJUSTMENT-6014.feedback: The indexed target is 40000×160/100=64000; the current 60000 falls 4000 short.
ECON-NL-INFLATION-ADJUSTMENT-6014.commonError: Compares nominal salaries without applying the CPI ratio.

ECON-NL-REAL-INTEREST-RATE-6015.q: Use the Fisher approximation. A loan fixes nominal interest at 9%. Expected inflation was 5%, but actual inflation is 7%. What realized real rate replaces the expected 4%?
ECON-NL-REAL-INTEREST-RATE-6015.feedback: Realized real interest≈9−7=2%; actual, rather than expected, inflation determines realized purchasing power.
ECON-NL-REAL-INTEREST-RATE-6015.commonError: Uses expected inflation for a realized real return.

ECON-NL-SUBSTITUTION-BIAS-6011.q: Beef becomes dearer relative to chicken. Households substitute chicken, but a fixed CPI basket keeps the old beef quantity. Relative to the cost of the adjusted purchasing pattern, what bias can result?
options: The basket measures only chicken inflation
The fixed basket overstates the cost increase
The fixed basket understates the cost increase
The basket automatically records the new chicken quantity
ECON-NL-SUBSTITUTION-BIAS-6011.$correct: The fixed basket overstates the cost increase
ECON-NL-SUBSTITUTION-BIAS-6011.feedback: The fixed basket misses the saving available from substitution toward relatively cheaper chicken.
ECON-NL-SUBSTITUTION-BIAS-6011.commonError: Assumes a fixed basket automatically incorporates consumer substitution.

ECON-NL-LABOR-FORCE-CALCULATION-6026.q: There are 90 employed and 10 unemployed. Four unemployed people stop searching; nobody else changes status. What is the new labor force?
ECON-NL-LABOR-FORCE-CALCULATION-6026.feedback: The four move from unemployed to outside the labor force.90+6=96; employment stays 90.
ECON-NL-LABOR-FORCE-CALCULATION-6026.commonError: Keeps discouraged nonsearchers in the labor force.

ECON-NL-UNEMPLOYMENT-RATE-6027.q: There are 152 employed and 8 unemployed. Two unemployed workers find jobs. What is the new unemployment rate?
ECON-NL-UNEMPLOYMENT-RATE-6027.feedback: The labor force stays 160 while unemployment becomes 6: 6/160=3.75%.
ECON-NL-UNEMPLOYMENT-RATE-6027.commonError: Reduces the labor-force denominator when an unemployed worker becomes employed.

ECON-NL-LABOR-FORCE-PARTICIPATION-6028.q: Adult population is 250 and the labor force 150. Ten previously nonparticipating adults start active job search without finding jobs. What is the new LFPR?
ECON-NL-LABOR-FORCE-PARTICIPATION-6028.feedback: Job seekers join the labor force: 160/250=64%. They need not already be employed to participate.
ECON-NL-LABOR-FORCE-PARTICIPATION-6028.commonError: Excludes active unemployed job seekers from participation.

ECON-NL-EMPLOYMENT-CLASSIFICATION-6029.q: A survey has 90 employed and 10 unemployed. One employed person cuts paid work to one hour while seeking full-time work. How do measured employment and unemployment change?
options: Employment: falls 1; unemployment: rises 1.
Employment: rises 1; unemployment: falls 1.
Employment: unchanged; unemployment: unchanged.
Employment: falls 1; unemployment: unchanged.
ECON-NL-EMPLOYMENT-CLASSIFICATION-6029.feedback: One paid hour still counts as employed under the stated status rule. Underemployment changes without changing these measured counts.
ECON-NL-EMPLOYMENT-CLASSIFICATION-6029.commonError: Incorrect inference: Employment: falls 1; unemployment: rises 1.

ECON-NL-CYCLICAL-UNEMPLOYMENT-6033.q: Sales fall economy-wide during recession and trained workers are laid off. If demand returns with skills still suitable, which unemployment component should most directly shrink?
options: Cyclical unemployment
Structural unemployment from obsolete skills
Frictional unemployment from voluntary job changes
Natural unemployment caused by permanent skill mismatch
ECON-NL-CYCLICAL-UNEMPLOYMENT-6033.feedback: The unemployment arose from weak aggregate demand rather than an enduring mismatch; recovery can reduce its cyclical component.
ECON-NL-CYCLICAL-UNEMPLOYMENT-6033.commonError: Attributes recession layoffs to a permanent skill mismatch.

ECON-NL-FRICTIONAL-UNEMPLOYMENT-6031.q: Two workers are unemployed: A is briefly between suitable jobs; B’s old occupation has disappeared and employers require skills B lacks. Which worker is more directly helped by retraining?
options: A, because all job search is structural mismatch
Both equally, because duration alone defines unemployment type
Neither, because training can affect only cyclical unemployment
B, because the problem is structural mismatch
ECON-NL-FRICTIONAL-UNEMPLOYMENT-6031.$correct: B, because the problem is structural mismatch
ECON-NL-FRICTIONAL-UNEMPLOYMENT-6031.feedback: B lacks the skills demanded in available jobs. A’s short search between suitable jobs is frictional; faster matching may help without retraining.
ECON-NL-FRICTIONAL-UNEMPLOYMENT-6031.commonError: Confuses job matching with structural skill mismatch.

ECON-NL-STRUCTURAL-UNEMPLOYMENT-6032.q: Automation removes jobs whose workers lack skills for new vacancies. A policy only boosts demand for output without changing skills. Which limit follows?
options: The skill mismatch may persist despite stronger demand
All mismatch disappears as soon as spending increases
Unemployment becomes frictional solely because demand rises
The workers leave the labor force automatically
ECON-NL-STRUCTURAL-UNEMPLOYMENT-6032.$correct: The skill mismatch may persist despite stronger demand
ECON-NL-STRUCTURAL-UNEMPLOYMENT-6032.feedback: More demand need not give displaced workers the skills needed for existing vacancies. A structural problem can require retraining or mobility.
ECON-NL-STRUCTURAL-UNEMPLOYMENT-6032.commonError: Assumes demand expansion directly removes a skill mismatch.

ECON-NL-UNIONS-EFFICIENCY-WAGES-6035.q: A firm pays above-market wages to reduce quits. Its wage bill rises $10,000 but recruiting and training costs fall $15,000. What net cost implication supports the efficiency-wage rationale?
options: Relevant costs rise $10,000 because turnover savings do not count
Relevant costs fall $15,000 with no wage cost
Relevant costs fall $5,000 despite higher wages
Relevant costs rise $25,000
ECON-NL-UNIONS-EFFICIENCY-WAGES-6035.$correct: Relevant costs fall $5,000 despite higher wages
ECON-NL-UNIONS-EFFICIENCY-WAGES-6035.feedback: Combine the wage increase and turnover saving: 10000−15000=−5000. Higher wages can reduce other costs.
ECON-NL-UNIONS-EFFICIENCY-WAGES-6035.commonError: Evaluates the wage increase without its turnover-cost offset.

ECON-SP-CALCULATE-REQUIRED-RESERVES-6004.q: In a hypothetical system with a 12.5% reserve requirement, a bank has $8,000 deposits and $1,200 reserves. How much exceeds required reserves?
ECON-SP-CALCULATE-REQUIRED-RESERVES-6004.commonError: Treats total reserves as excess reserves.

LG-B-6003.q: In a hypothetical system with a 12% reserve requirement, a bank has $900,000 deposits and $100,000 reserves. What reserve adjustment meets the requirement?
options: Obtain $8,000 additional reserves
Lend $8,000 of excess reserves
Obtain $108,000 additional reserves
Lend $100,000 because all reserves are excess
LG-B-6003.feedback: Required reserves=.12×900000=108000. Existing reserves 100000 leave a shortfall 8000.
LG-B-6003.commonError: Confuses a reserve shortfall with lending capacity.

LG-B-6005.q: In a hypothetical system initially at required reserves, a $10,000 currency deposit enters with rr=20%. Banks lend all excess reserves and all payments are redeposited, with no other constraints. Total deposits can rise $50,000 including the initial deposit. What is the net increase in currency-plus-checking money?
LG-B-6005.feedback: Deposits rise 50000 but currency held by the public falls 10000. Net currency-plus-checking money rises 40000.
LG-B-6005.commonError: Counts the initial currency-to-deposit conversion as net new money.

ECON-SP-CENTRAL-BANK-ROLE-6002.q: A solvent bank faces a temporary withdrawal surge and cannot quickly sell assets. Which central-bank function could address the liquidity problem?
options: Lender-of-last-resort lending against acceptable collateral
Directly setting household income-tax rates
Making the bank’s owners immune from all investment losses
Recording the bank’s withdrawals as government purchases
ECON-SP-CENTRAL-BANK-ROLE-6002.feedback: Emergency liquidity lending can help a solvent bank meet withdrawals. It is distinct from tax policy or guaranteeing shareholders against losses.
ECON-SP-CENTRAL-BANK-ROLE-6002.commonError: Confuses temporary liquidity support with fiscal authority or capital guarantees.

LG-B-6002.q: Officials propose changing the policy interest-rate setting, while legislators propose a purchases increase. Which institution-policy pairing is appropriate?
options: Fiscal authorities for rates; central bank for public purchases
Central bank for the rate decision; fiscal authorities for purchases
Central bank for both because all stabilization is monetary
Legislators for both because rates are a spending item
LG-B-6002.$correct: Central bank for the rate decision; fiscal authorities for purchases
LG-B-6002.feedback: Interest-rate policy is monetary; government spending is fiscal. The implementation authority follows the instrument used.
LG-B-6002.commonError: Confuses monetary and fiscal policy authority.

ECON-SP-LIMITS-OF-MONETARY-CONTROL-6008.q: A reserve injection could support $1,000 of deposits in the simple maximum model. Banks instead retain additional excess reserves. Relative to that maximum, what should an analyst forecast?
options: No reserves remaining because deposits remove reserves from the system
Less deposit creation, other conditions equal
More deposit creation because excess reserves are loans
Exactly $1,000 regardless of lending decisions
ECON-SP-LIMITS-OF-MONETARY-CONTROL-6008.$correct: Less deposit creation, other conditions equal
ECON-SP-LIMITS-OF-MONETARY-CONTROL-6008.feedback: Additional reserve retention leaves less available for repeated lending and deposit expansion than the restrictive simple maximum assumes.
ECON-SP-LIMITS-OF-MONETARY-CONTROL-6008.commonError: Treats the simple multiplier maximum as guaranteed actual expansion.

LG-B-6008.q: A $100 reserve injection is followed by $400 in additional deposits. The simple model with rr=10% predicts $1,000. Which observed multiplier should be used to describe this episode?
options: 10, because the legal ratio fixes actual expansion
0.25, because reserves are divided by deposits
40, because both quantities must be expressed as percentages
4, below the simple maximum 10
LG-B-6008.feedback: Observed deposit expansion per reserve dollar=400/100=4. Leakages or other lending constraints can leave it below 10.
LG-B-6008.commonError: Substitutes the simple theoretical multiplier for the observed ratio.

ECON-SP-VALUE-OF-MONEY-6012.q: The price level rises from 2 to 5. Using value of money=1/P, how many units of the reference basket can $10 buy afterward?
options: 2 units
5 units
20 units
50 units
ECON-SP-VALUE-OF-MONEY-6012.feedback: At P=5 each dollar buys 1/5 basket unit; 10/5=2 units.
ECON-SP-VALUE-OF-MONEY-6012.commonError: Multiplies cash by the price level to measure purchasing power.

LG-B-6009.q: Money’s value falls from 1/2 to 1/4 basket unit per dollar. What happens to the dollars needed to buy one unchanged basket?
options: They rise from $0.50 to $0.75
They stay $2 because the basket is unchanged
They rise from $2 to $4
They fall from $4 to $2
LG-B-6009.feedback: The basket price is the reciprocal of money’s value: 2 then 4.
LG-B-6009.commonError: Uses the value-of-money fraction directly as the basket price.

LG-B-6010.q: Use the quantity-theory growth approximation. Money grows 12% and output 4%. If velocity now falls 2% rather than staying stable, what inflation rate is predicted?
LG-B-6010.feedback: Inflation≈gM+gV−gY=12−2−4=6%. The velocity decline lowers spending growth.
LG-B-6010.commonError: Ignores a stated change in velocity.

ECON-SP-MONETARY-NEUTRALITY-6014.q: All nominal prices double in a long-run neutrality comparison. A worker’s nominal wage also doubles from $20 to $40. What happens to the real wage?
options: It rises by $20 of purchasing power
It is unchanged
It doubles
It halves
ECON-SP-MONETARY-NEUTRALITY-6014.feedback: Real wage=W/P. Doubling numerator and denominator leaves the ratio unchanged.
ECON-SP-MONETARY-NEUTRALITY-6014.commonError: Treats a nominal wage rise as a real gain when prices rise proportionately.

LG-B-6012.q: In a long-run neutrality comparison money, nominal GDP and the price level all double. What happens to real GDP=nominal GDP/(price index/100)?
options: It remains unchanged
It doubles
It quadruples
It falls by half
LG-B-6012.feedback: Proportional nominal GDP and price increases cancel in the real-output ratio.
LG-B-6012.commonError: Counts a proportional price increase as real output growth.

ECON-SP-FISHER-EFFECT-6015.q: Using the Fisher approximation, expected inflation rises from 6% to 8% while the expected real rate remains 2%. What new nominal rate is consistent with both conditions?
ECON-SP-FISHER-EFFECT-6015.commonError: Holds the nominal rate fixed despite higher expected inflation and a fixed real rate.

LG-B-6013.q: A contract quotes 8% nominal interest and expected inflation 6%. If a new contract has expected inflation 3% with the same expected real return, what nominal rate should it quote?
LG-B-6013.feedback: Original expected real return≈8−6=2%; new nominal≈2+3=5%.
LG-B-6013.commonError: Changes nominal and expected inflation in opposite directions at a fixed real rate.

ECON-SP-INFLATION-TAX-6018.q: A household holds $100 cash as prices rise 10%. It receives no interest. How does this illustrate the inflation tax on money holders?
options: The same cash buys less, about $90.91 in initial-price purchasing power
The cash balance automatically rises to $110
Real purchasing power rises 10% because nominal cash is unchanged
The household owes a separate $10 statutory income-tax bill
ECON-SP-INFLATION-TAX-6018.$correct: The same cash buys less, about $90.91 in initial-price purchasing power
ECON-SP-INFLATION-TAX-6018.feedback: Real cash purchasing power is 100/1.10≈90.91. The loss need not appear as a separate tax bill.
ECON-SP-INFLATION-TAX-6018.commonError: Treats inflation tax as an explicit statutory tax payment.

ECON-SP-MENU-COSTS-6017.q: Inflation leads a shop to reprint signs at $200 per update. Updates rise from 2 to 6 per year. What additional annual resource cost is a menu cost?
ECON-SP-MENU-COSTS-6017.feedback: Four additional updates cost 4×200=800. The cost is changing posted prices, not the price increase itself.
ECON-SP-MENU-COSTS-6017.commonError: Confuses total repricing costs with the added cost requested.

ECON-SP-SHOELEATHER-COSTS-6016.q: To avoid holding cash during inflation, a household makes four extra bank trips per month, each taking 30 minutes. What monthly time cost illustrates shoeleather costs?
options: 4 hours
0.5 hour
120 hours
2 hours
ECON-SP-SHOELEATHER-COSTS-6016.feedback: Four trips×30 minutes=120 minutes=2 hours spent managing balances.
ECON-SP-SHOELEATHER-COSTS-6016.commonError: Counts only one trip or confuses minutes with hours.

LG-B-6014.q: Use the Fisher approximation. A fixed nominal loan pays 9%; expected inflation was 3%, actual inflation 10%. Compared with the expected 6% real return, who benefits from the surprise?
options: The borrower; realized real interest remains 6%
Neither; actual inflation cannot change a fixed nominal contract’s real value
The borrower; realized real interest is about−1%
The lender; realized real interest is about 19%
LG-B-6014.$correct: The borrower; realized real interest is about−1%
LG-B-6014.feedback: Realized return≈9−10=−1%, seven points below the expected 6%. The borrower repays less purchasing power than anticipated.
LG-B-6014.commonError: Uses expected rather than actual inflation to measure realized return.

LG-B-6015.q: A store spends $600 updating prices while a household loses three hours making extra cash-management trips. Which comparison identifies the two resource costs?
options: Both are changes in real GDP caused solely by counting cash
The store incurs menu costs; the household incurs shoeleather costs
The store incurs shoeleather costs; the household incurs menu costs
Both are transfers from lenders to borrowers
LG-B-6015.$correct: The store incurs menu costs; the household incurs shoeleather costs
LG-B-6015.feedback: Repricing resources are menu costs; extra balance-management effort is shoeleather cost. Both use resources beyond a mere transfer between borrowers and lenders.
LG-B-6015.commonError: Reverses repricing and cash-management cost categories.

ECON-SP-EXPLAIN-AD-SLOPE-6019.q: With nominal money supply fixed, the price level falls. Apply the interest-rate channel of the AD slope: what happens to money demand, interest and investment?
options: Money supply rises, interest rises, investment rises
Money demand falls, interest rises, investment falls
Money demand falls, interest falls, investment rises
Money demand rises, interest rises, investment falls
ECON-SP-EXPLAIN-AD-SLOPE-6019.$correct: Money demand falls, interest falls, investment rises
ECON-SP-EXPLAIN-AD-SLOPE-6019.feedback: Lower transaction-price needs reduce nominal money demand, lowering the interest rate and encouraging investment. The money supply was held fixed.
ECON-SP-EXPLAIN-AD-SLOPE-6019.commonError: Reverses the money-demand response to a lower price level.

ECON-SP-IDENTIFY-AD-SHIFTERS-6020.q: Business investment falls for reasons unrelated to the price level. With upward-sloping SRAS unchanged, what short-run output/price combination follows from the AD shift?
options: Output falls while the price level rises
Both output and the price level rise
Both output and the price level fall
Output rises while the price level falls
ECON-SP-IDENTIFY-AD-SHIFTERS-6020.$correct: Both output and the price level fall
ECON-SP-IDENTIFY-AD-SHIFTERS-6020.feedback: Lower autonomous investment shifts AD left; along unchanged SRAS the new equilibrium has lower output and prices.
ECON-SP-IDENTIFY-AD-SHIFTERS-6020.commonError: Mistakes an adverse demand shift for an adverse supply shift.

ECON-SP-IDENTIFY-SRAS-SHIFTERS-6023.q: Oil costs fall while aggregate demand is unchanged. What output/price combination follows from the resulting SRAS shift?
options: Both output and the price level rise
Output falls and the price level rises
Both output and the price level fall
Output rises and the price level falls
ECON-SP-IDENTIFY-SRAS-SHIFTERS-6023.$correct: Output rises and the price level falls
ECON-SP-IDENTIFY-SRAS-SHIFTERS-6023.feedback: Lower input costs shift SRAS right, increasing output and reducing the price level at the new demand intersection.
ECON-SP-IDENTIFY-SRAS-SHIFTERS-6023.commonError: Uses demand-shift price/output signs for a supply improvement.

ECON-SP-EXPECTED-PRICE-SRAS-SHIFT-6024.q: Expected prices rise and new wage contracts raise nominal costs. With aggregate demand fixed, apply the SRAS shift to output and the price level.
options: Output rises and the price level falls
Output and the price level both fall
Output falls and the price level rises
Output and the price level both rise
ECON-SP-EXPECTED-PRICE-SRAS-SHIFT-6024.$correct: Output falls and the price level rises
ECON-SP-EXPECTED-PRICE-SRAS-SHIFT-6024.feedback: Higher expected wages/costs shift SRAS left. The intersection with unchanged AD has lower output and higher prices.
ECON-SP-EXPECTED-PRICE-SRAS-SHIFT-6024.commonError: Treats higher expected costs as an increase in short-run supply.

ECON-SP-IDENTIFY-LRAS-6021.q: Technology raises potential output from 100 to 110. If actual output stays 100, what output gap exists relative to the new LRAS?
options: A110-unit recessionary gap
A10-unit recessionary gap
A10-unit inflationary gap
No gap because actual output did not change
ECON-SP-IDENTIFY-LRAS-6021.feedback: The benchmark rose:actual 100−potential 110=−10. A capacity gain can open a shortfall if demand does not keep pace.
ECON-SP-IDENTIFY-LRAS-6021.commonError: Uses the old potential-output benchmark after a capacity change.

ECON-SP-CLASSIFY-OUTPUT-GAP-6027.q: Actual output is $19 trillion and potential $20 trillion. If demand increases output by $0.5 trillion without changing capacity, what gap remains?
options: No gap because output rose
A $0.5 trillion recessionary gap
A $0.5 trillion inflationary gap
A $1.5 trillion recessionary gap
ECON-SP-CLASSIFY-OUTPUT-GAP-6027.feedback: New actual output 19.5 remains 0.5 below potential 20.
ECON-SP-CLASSIFY-OUTPUT-GAP-6027.commonError: Confuses a partial recovery with complete gap closure.

ECON-SP-EXPLAIN-LONG-RUN-ADJUSTMENT-6028.q: Output is above potential, but wage adjustment is slow. A proposed demand stimulus would arrive before self-correction. How would that stimulus initially affect the existing gap, other conditions equal?
options: It would permanently raise LRAS by the size of the stimulus
It would enlarge the positive output gap
It would directly lower expected wages and close the gap
It would reduce aggregate demand and close the gap
ECON-SP-EXPLAIN-LONG-RUN-ADJUSTMENT-6028.$correct: It would enlarge the positive output gap
ECON-SP-EXPLAIN-LONG-RUN-ADJUSTMENT-6028.feedback: Extra demand at an already above-potential starting point pushes activity further above capacity before wage adjustment.
ECON-SP-EXPLAIN-LONG-RUN-ADJUSTMENT-6028.commonError: Applies recession stimulus to an inflationary output gap.

ECON-SP-CHOOSE-STABILIZATION-RESPONSE-60.q: After a demand recession, falling wages are already shifting SRAS right toward recovery. A stimulus takes a year to arrive. What fact is most relevant to whether it will stabilize output at arrival?
options: Only the size of the gap when the recession began
Whether the original shock was measured in dollars
Whether the economy has ever used fiscal policy before
The expected remaining gap when the stimulus arrives
ECON-SP-CHOOSE-STABILIZATION-RESPONSE-60.$correct: The expected remaining gap when the stimulus arrives
ECON-SP-CHOOSE-STABILIZATION-RESPONSE-60.feedback: Compare the intervention with conditions at implementation. Existing self-correction can reduce or eliminate the gap before delayed stimulus arrives.
ECON-SP-CHOOSE-STABILIZATION-RESPONSE-60.commonError: Targets a historical gap without allowing for recovery during the policy lag.

ECON-SP-TRACE-SUPPLY-SHOCK-6026.q: An oil-price spike shifts SRAS left. Authorities then expand demand to support output. Relative to leaving demand fixed, what additional tradeoff follows?
options: Demand expansion lowers output further while reducing prices
Higher output support comes with additional price pressure
Output support also necessarily restores the original low price level
Demand expansion shifts SRAS back directly with no price effect
ECON-SP-TRACE-SUPPLY-SHOCK-6026.$correct: Higher output support comes with additional price pressure
ECON-SP-TRACE-SUPPLY-SHOCK-6026.feedback: Expansion moves along the worse supply relation. It can support output but does not remove the higher production costs.
ECON-SP-TRACE-SUPPLY-SHOCK-6026.commonError: Treats demand support as a direct reversal of a supply shock.

ECON-SP-MONEY-DEMAND-INTEREST-RATE-6030.q: Income rises and money demand increases, with money supply fixed. If investment is interest-sensitive, what follow-on pressure results?
options: Higher interest raises investment
Investment is unchanged by assumption whenever income changes
Higher interest reduces investment
Lower interest raises investment
ECON-SP-MONEY-DEMAND-INTEREST-RATE-6030.feedback: Greater money demand raises the equilibrium rate; the higher financing cost reduces interest-sensitive investment.

LG-B-6017.q: Money demand rises at fixed supply. A firm borrows at the resulting market interest rate. Relative to before the shift, what happens to its financing cost?
options: It falls as the equilibrium interest rate rises
It falls because demand for money means demand for bonds rises
It stays fixed because money demand cannot affect rates
It rises as the equilibrium interest rate rises
